PREFACE 

The rapidity with which changes in the formal aspects of the law have been made in the past few years is amazing. Not only has the Legislature been especially productive, but the Supreme Court has taken a hand in adding to the forms of procedure. 

The editors have attempted to continue the tradition of these volumes by reflecting these changes as they occur. It has been necessary to re-write in their entirety such subjects as Corporations and Interpleader; to completely revise Bankruptcy, Building and Loan Associations, and many others; to delete Account Render, Detinue and Dower; and to add Bulk Sales, Joinder of 

Defendants, Juvenile Courts and Minors. 

It is hoped that in rendering this service to the Bar these familiar volumes may remain the steadfast companions and tools of the active practitioner. April 10, 1934. 

THE EDITORS.

DUNLAP'S BOOK OF FORMS ACCOUNT RENDER 

(The ancient action of account render is abolished by the Act of 31 May, 1933, P. L. 1090; courts of equity now have jurisdiction in matters formerly covered by this action. See 

EQUITY.) ACCOUNTS See DECEDENTS' ESTATES and ASSIGNMENTS FOR BENEFIT OF CREDITORS as to procedure relating to accounts. 

Forms are given for the accounts of Executors, Administrators, Trustees and Guardians.

Accounts of Executors and Administrators and final accounts of Guardians are filed in the office of the Register of Wills and must be advertised. Accounts of Testamentary Trustees are filed in the Orphans' Court, as are the triennial accounts of Guardians.

Accounts of Executors and Administrators should be filed six months after the advertising of the grant of Letters. Guardians are obliged to file accounts for inspection every three years. 

The final account of a guardian should cover the entire period of the guardianship. 

It is essential that there be no blending of principal and income, administration and distribution or realty and personalty. 

Real estate if appearing in an account should, as a general rule, be the subject of separate statement. 7

ACCOUNTS 

When separate Orphans' Courts exist, such accounts as properly come before them are audited by the court; in other counties an auditor may be appointed. 

The court will not audit an account or decree a distribution until six months has expired after the grant of letters.

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS ACKNOWLEDGMENTS PENNSYLVANIA 

Acknowledgements. Within the state before a justice of the supreme court, judges of the court of common pleas, mayors and magistrates, recorders of deeds, notaries public, justices of the peace, or commissioners of deeds for this commonwealth. 

A justice of the peace may now take an acknowledgment anywhere in the state even though outside his own district or county; Act of 20 May, 1931, P. L. 139.

Without the State by a judge of the United States supreme or district court, by the mayor or chief magistrate of the town, or place where the deed is executed, under the public seal, a judge of the supreme or superior court, or court of common pleas if certified under the hand of the judge and seal of the court, or a commissioner for Pennsylvania, a notary public having a seal, or any officer of any state authorized by its laws to take acknowledgments, a certificate of his authority being annexed.

Acknowledgments may also be taken under the provisions of the acts of 22 April, 1863, P. L. 572, and 21

May, 1901, P. L. 271, by officers in the military service of the United States, in Cuba, Porto Rico and the Philippine Islands or other possessions of the United States, holding the rank of major or any higher rank. 

Without the United States by ambassadors, ministers plenipotentiary, chargés d'affaires, or by other persons exercising public ministerial functions duly appointed by the United States, by foreign commissioners in chancery, or by a notary public, or by commissioners appointed by the governor under the act of 21 April, 1856, P. L. 484.

Dower and curtesy exist and may be barred by joinder of husband and wife in the same deed.

ALABAMA 

Acknowledgments.—Within the state may be taken by judges of the supreme and circuit courts and the clerks of such courts, by chancellors, registers in chancery, judges of the courts of probate, justices of the peace, and notaries public.

Without the state by judges and clerks of any federal court, judges and clerks of any court of record in any state, notaries public, or commissioners appointed by the governor of this state.

Without the United States by the judge of any court of record, mayor or chief magistrate of any city, town, borough, or county, notaries public, or by any diplomatic, consular or commercial agent of the United States. 

The husband must join with wife in conveyances which must be attested by two witnesses or acknowledged. 

Dower exists and may be released by the wife joining her husband in the conveyance, or in a power of attorney to convey, in presence of two witnesses, or acknowledging the deed. 

Curtesy.-Does not exist. 

Seals.-None required.

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS 

Witnesses. None required except to prove deed not acknowledged.

A conveyance may be admitted to record on proof, if attested by two witnesses.

ALASKA TERRITORY 

Deeds executed according to the laws of the various states are valid. 

Acknowledgments. Within the territory may be taken before a judge, clerk of the district court, notary public or commissioner. The officer taking the acknowledgment must endorse thereon a certificate of acknowledgment and the true date of making the same under his hand. 

Without the territory before any judge of a court of record, justice of the peace, notary public, or other officer authorized by the laws of the state to take acknowledgments, or before any commissioner appointed for such purpose.

Without the United States before any United States minister or consul or notary public attested by his seal.

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS 

Officer taking acknowledgment must know or have proof of identity of person appearing before him. 

If the acknowledgment be not taken before a commissioner or a notary public certified under his notarial seal, or before a clerk of a court of record certified under the seal of the court, such deed shall have attached a certificate of the clerk or other proper certifying officer of a court of record of the county or district within which the acknowledgment was taken, that the person taking the same was as he is represented to be, and that he believes the signature of such person subscribed thereto to be genuine, and that the deed is executed and acknowledged according to the laws of such State. 

Dower and Curtesy exist.

Seals. Required. 

ARIZONA 

Acknowledgments.—Within the state, before a clerk of a court, having a seal, a notary public, a county recorder or justice of the peace.

Without the state, by a clerk of some court of record having a seal, or by any commissioner of deeds appointed by the governor, or a notary public.

Without the United States, by a minister, commissioner, or chargé d'affaires, a consul-general, consul, vice consul, commercial agent, vice-commercial agent, deputy consul, or consular agent of the United States, resident in the country where the acknowledgment is made, or a notary public. The officer taking the acknowledgment must affix his official seal. 

A married woman has the same rights over her separate property as though sole but must join her husband in sale of homestead or common property. 

The acknowledgment of a married woman, when required by law, may be taken in the same form as if she

ARKANSAS 

Acknowledgments. Within the state before the supreme court or circuit court, or either of the judges thereof, or the clerk of any court of record, or before any justice of the peace or notary public. 

Without the state, before any court of the United States, or of any state or colony, possession or dependency of the United States having a seal, or the clerk of such court, notary public, mayor of a town or city, or commissioner appointed by the governor of this state. 

Without the United States, before a United States consul, or court of any state, kingdom or empire having a seal, or any mayor or chief officer of any city or town having an official seal, or before any officer of any foreign country who, by the laws of such country, is authorized to take probate of the conveyance of real estate of his own country, if he have an official seal. 

The execution of an unacknowledged deed may be proved by one or more of the subscribing witnesses. Acknowledgments in all cases should be attested by the official seal of the officer taking them; if, when taken within the United States, such officer have no seal of office, then under the official signature of such officer. 

Married women have the same rights over their separate property as though sole, though curtesy exists in all real estate of which they die seized. Dower exists and may be barred by joining with her husband in a deed. 

Seals. None required.

CALIFORNIA 

Acknowledgments.-Within the state may be made at any place within the state before a justice or clerk of the supreme court, or judge of a superior court, or within the city, county, or township for which the officer was elected or appointed, a court commissioner, notary public, or a justice of the peace, a clerk of a court of record, or a county recorder.

Without the state, before a justice, judge, or clerk of any court of record of the United States, a justice, judge or clerk of any court of record of any state, a commissioner appointed by the governor of this state for that purpose, a notary public, or any other officer of the state where the acknowledgment is made, authorized by its laws to take such proof or acknowledgment. 

Without the United States, before a minister, commissioner, or chargé d'affaires of the United States, resident and accredited in the country where the proof or acknowledgment is made, or, a consul, vice-consul or consular agent of the United States, resident in the country where the proof or acknowledgment is made; or a judge of a court of record of the country, where the proof or acknowledgment is made; or commissioners appointed for such purposes by the governor of this state, pursuant to special statutes; or a notary public. Where any of the foregoing officers are permitted to appoint deputies, such deputies may act in the name of the principal. 

The officer taking an acknowledgment should know or have satisfactory evidence, on the oath or affirmation of a credible witness, that the person making such acknowledgment is the individual who is described in and who executed the instrument, or, if executed by a corporation, that the person making such acknowledgment is the

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS 

president or secretary of such corporation or other person who executed it on its behalf. 

Officers taking and certifying acknowledgments, etc., must authenticate their certificates by affixing thereto their signatures, followed by the names of their offices; also, their seals of office, if required by the laws of their state or country to have official seals. 

When not acknowledged, proof may be made, by the parties executing the instrument or either of them; by a subscribing witness; or by proof of the handwriting of the party and of a subscribing witness, where the parties are dead, nonresidents, &c. 

There being no dower or curtesy there need be no joinder of husband and wife as to their separate property though they must join in a deed of the homstead. 

A wife has the same rights over her separate property as if sole. 

Seals. None required.

Witnesses.-None necessary.

such state or of the United States within such state, having a seal, such clerk certifying the acknowledgment under the seal of such court; a notary public under his notarial seal; any commissioner of deeds for this state under his hand and official seal; before any other officer authorized by the laws of such state to take such acknowledgment, the latter having affixed thereto a certificate by the clerk of some court of record of the county, city or district, wherein such officer resides, under the seal of such court, that the person certifying such acknowledgment is the officer he assumes to be, that he has the authority, by the laws of such state, to take and certify such acknowledgment, and that the signature of such officer to the certificate of acknowledgment is the true signature of such officer.

Without the United States, before any court of record having a seal, the acknowledgment being certified by the judge or justice of such court to have been made before such court, and such certificate to be attested by the seal of such court; before the mayor, or other chief officer, of any city or town having a seal, such mayor or other chief officer certifying such acknowledgment under such seal; before any consul of the United States within such foreign country, under the seal of his consulate. 

Deeds not acknowledged may be proved before an officer authorized to take acknowledgments upon the testimony of at least one competent credible witness that the person offering to prove the execution of such deed or writing is a subscribing witness thereto. The officer taking acknowledgment must know or have proof of the identity of the person appearing before him. 

Dower and Curtesy do not exist. A married woman has the same rights over her separate property as if sole, though she must join in a sale or mortgage of the homestead and be separately examined.

Acknowledgments. Within the state, before a judge of a court of record of this state or of the United States; a clerk of the superior court, court of common pleas, or

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS 

district court, justice of the peace, commissioner of the school fund, commissioner of the superior court, notary public, either with or without his official seal, town clerk, or assistant town clerk.

Without the state, before a commissioner appointed by the governor of this state or any officer authorized to take acknowledgments in such state. 

Without the United States, before any ambassador, minister, chargé d'affaires, consul, vice-consul, deputy consul, consul-general, vice-consul-general, commercial agent or vice-commercial agent of the United States, notary public, or justice of the peace, no officer having power to take such acknowledgment except within the territorial limits in which he may perform the proper duties of his office.

Conveyances of real estate situated in this state and powers of attorney therefor, executed and acknowledged in any other state or territory in conformity with its laws relative to the conveyance of lands therein situated, shall be valid.

All conveyances of the real estate of wives married prior to April 20, 1877, which are executed by them jointly with their husbands, and duly acknowledged and recorded, shall be valid and effectual to transfer such estate; and all conveyances, by the husband alone, of the real estate of such a wife, shall be ineffectual to convey her interest therein, but no joinder by the husband shall be required in case of a wife married on or after said date. On the death of a husband or wife married on or after the 20th day of April, 1877, the survivor shall be entitled to the use for life of one-third in value of all property real and personal, legally or equitably owned by the other at the time of his or her death, after the payment of all debts and charges against the estate. The right to such third shall not be defeated by any disposition of the property by will, to other parties, but where there is no will, the survivor shall take such third

ILLINOIS 

Acknowledgments. Within the state, before a master in chancery, notary public under his seal, United States commissioner under his seal, county clerk, justice of the peace of the county where the lands lie, any court of record having a seal, or judge, justice or clerk thereof, attested by the seal of the court. 

Without the state, before a justice of the peace, notary public, master in chancery, United States commissioner, commissioner of deeds, mayor of a city, clerk of a county, any judge, justice, clerk, or deputy clerk of the supreme, circuit, superior, district, county, common pleas, probate, orphans' or surrogate's court in conformity with the laws of the state where made; a certificate of authority by the clerk of a court of record being attached. A certificate of authority should be attached where taken by a justice of the peace, or master in chancery. If taken by the mayor of a city it must be under the city seal and if by a clerk or other officer of the court, under the seal of that court.

Without the United States, before any court having a seal, any judge, justice or clerk thereof, notary public, commissioner, ambassador, minister, secretary of legation, consul, vice-consul, deputy consul, commercial or consular agent of the United States in any foreign country, attested by his official seal, or before any officer authorized by the laws of such place having a seal. Such acknowledgments should be certified by a consul or other officer of the United States to have been taken in accordance with such laws.

Instruments not acknowledged may be proved by a subscribing witness or, where grantor and subscribing witnesses cannot be had, by proof of the handwriting of the grantor and one subscribing witness.

Without the United States before a minister, chargé d'affaires, consul, or before any officer of such country who is authorized by its laws to take acknowledgment or proof of conveyances, attested by the official seal of such officer.

If not attested by the officer's official seal (when taken within the United States) a certificate of authority by the clerk of a court of record under the seal of the court must be attached.

Dower and Curtesy.-Neither exists. 

Married women cannot convey or encumber their real estate without the joinder of their husbands. Husband and wife should join in all deeds. Separate examination not required.

Seals.-None necessary. 

Witnesses.-None required.

ACQUITTANCE SEE RECEIPTS; RELEASE 

An acquittance is an agreement in writing to discharge a party from an engagement to pay a sum of money; it is evidence of payment. It differs from a release in this, that the latter must be under seal, while an acquittance is not under seal. In 

Pennsylvania a receipt, though not under seal, has nearly the same effect as a release. But if not under seal it is necessary to show the consideration thereof. See Act of 1927, P. L. 985.

Acquittance for Money Received on a Sale of Land 

KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS, that I, John Jones, of Erie, in the County of Erie and State of Pennsylvania, do hereby acknowledge myself, upon the day of the date hereof, to have received of William Burns, of Concord,

ACQUITTANCE 

101 county and state aforesaid, the sum of one hundred dollars, being the last payment, and in full, of five hundred dollars by him paid as the consideration of the purchase of a certain tract of land, situate in Concord aforesaid, and bounded by lands of -, containing fifty acres of land, be the same more or less, and by me the said John Jones sold and conveyed to the said William Burns. 

And of the said whole sum of five hundred dollars, and every part and parcel thereof, I, the said John Jones, do by these presents, for me, my heirs, executors and administrators, acquit and discharge the said William Burns, his heirs, executors and administrators forever. 

In testimony whereof, I have hereunto set my hand, this day of

JOHN JONES.

3. On Wednesday, the 

1929, at about four o'clock P. M. a collision occured between the steamship Bailey and Reyburn, on the high seas, about a mile and a half southwest of Cape May, N. J., by reason of which the Bailey sustained severe damage. 

4. Upon information and belief, the libellant alleges that the following are the circumstances of the collision: [Describe circumstances of collision in detail]. 

5. Libellant alleges that the collision and consequent damage was in no way due to any fault on the part of the steamship Bailey which was in all respects properly and carefully managed and navigated, but due to the fault of the steamship Reyburn in the following amongst other particulars which will be pointed out on the trial of this action: 

(a) In that she was navigated at too great speed in a fog. (b) In that she did not give proper heed to the signals of the Bailey. (c) In that she did not stop and reverse her engines in time as she should have done. (d) In that she did not have a proper and efficient lookout. (e) In that her master and officers were incompetent and inattentive to their duties. (f) In that she was equipped with turbine engines which could not be reversed in time to prevent the collision. (g) In that she failed to stop when the fog signals of the Bailey were first heard. 

6. Libellant further alleges by reason of said collision he has suffered damages to the steamship Bailey with her cargo, and on account of the expenses arising out of said collision, in a sum which libellant is at present, unable to state with accuracy, but which, upon information and belief, will amount to one hundred thousand ($100,000) dollars.

The libel of A. B. against the British steamship S. S., whereof X. Y. is master, her tackle, apparel and furniture, and against all persons intervening for their interest therein, in a cause of salvage, civil and maritime, alleges as follows: 

9. Libel In Rem for Salvage 

1. The libellant is engaged in the wrecking business in all its branches, and carry it on as a profession in all its various departments. Their operations extend, when needed or demanded, into all the navigable waters and along all the dangerous coasts of the globe. Their own equipment and outfit is large and costly, subject to rapid deterioration and danger of loss, and is mainly of a character which is only useful in such business. The vessels owned by them are built for and specially adapted to the wrecking business aforesaid, and are provided with wrecking apparatus of every kind of the most approved pattern and invention. Both masters and mariners are trained for the wrecking business and are skillful and daring. In addition to the property owned by him the libellant constantly employ chartered vessels at high cost. 

All the said vessels, whether owned or chartered by the libellant their officers, crews and other employees, are under the control and direction of the libellant, who alone are entitled to receive the salvage rewards earned by them. 

2. The said steamship S. S. is a modern English steamer with triple expansion engines, gross tonnage net tonnage built of steel, feet 9 long, feet beam, feet depth of hold, and is equipped with all modern improvements, and a steamer of high value. 

3. The said steamer at some time during the night of went ashore abreast of on the

SALVAGE 

119 The place at which she went ashore is on the well-known dangerous coast, with no harbor in of the immediate vincinity. [Describe situation.] 

4. The next morning at o'clock the libellant, at his station, received information of the disaster. The steamer which was lying at the wharf with steam up, ready to proceed to the immediate assistance of distressed vessels, as is libellant's custom, was at once dispatched to the assistance of the distressed vessel. She arrived at the wreck at and found the steamer broadside on the beach, heading to the northward. Although there was a heavy sea, a boat was at once launched, and Captain the commander, boarded the ship and arranged to lay anchor and cables and render all necessary assistance. [Here describe in detail what was done.] 5. In this manner the salvage operation was attended with complete success. The steamer, which was thoroughly disabled by the loss of her rudder post, the breaking of the blades of her propellor, the loss of part of her stern post and feet of her keel and the breaking of her plates, and which was so far in shore that the hope of her ever regaining her native elements seemed visionary, was gotten off without additional injury to that which she had sustained from her own acts, and safely delivered in a safe port.

During the operation a large amount of property, consisting of anchors, cables, ropes and all other property used by wreckers, was in constant risk in the most inclement season of the year and in one of the most dangerous points on the coast, and more important still, the wrecking crew, which consisted of Captain in charge, as foreman and ten experienced wreckers, in addition to the regular crews of two steamers, were in constant danger of life and limb during the inclement weather and high seas which prevailed, and but for the promptness, skill and industry with which this service was rendered, the vessel would have been a total loss.

6. The total value of the property actually employed by the libellants in the service is very great, certainly not less than $ The total number of men employed by the libellant, including the crews of the two steamers, was about forty. The value of the steamer saved, in her condition when delivered at is also very great, she being a first-class modern steamer, and her injuries, if serious, being easily capable of repair, and the libellant on information and belief states that her value is about the sum of $- 8. The libellant thereupon consented to render such assistance as was in his power, and for that purpose let go his anchor and got out hawsers to said brig, and by constant heaving, prevented her working further up into the said, and at high water, succeeded in heaving her off without injury. Thereupon the master of the brig informed the libellant that he was bound to sea, and desirous of not being delayed, and that he would give the libellant a letter to his owner, the respondent A. B., who would pay him his reasonable salvage. The said master thereupon gave the libellant a letter to said respondent, informing him that the libellant had rendered to the brig S. S. valuable assistance and was entitled to salvage. 

4. The libellant therefore consented to allow the said brig to pursue her voyage, and on his arrival in the port

ADMIRALTY 

of he presented said letter to said owner, and for himself and his ship's company, and his owners, whose ship had been periled in rendering such assistance, and offered to accept the sum of five hundred dollars, if paid without delay or trouble to the libellant, although as he had previously been informed, said brig and cargo were worth the sum of thirty thousand dollars, and the said sum of five hundred dolars was an inadequate salvage compensation, but said owner refused to pay the same, or to pay any more than fifty dollars. 

5. All and singular the premises are true and within the admiralty and maritime jurisdiction of the U. S. and of this Honorable Court. 

WHEREFORE, the libellant prays that citation in due form of law may issue against the said A. 5. That the said accident was caused without any fault or negligence on the part of the libellant and solely by the defective, unsafe, and unseaworthy condition of the vessel and by the fault and negligence of the master and crew of the said steamship as follows: [Set forth specific allegations of negligence.] 

6. That by reason of the aforesaid the libellant has sustained severe injuries to his back, head, etc. 

7. That by reason of the aforesaid the libellant has and will probably in the future suffer great pain and agony; that he has and will probably in the future be unable to attend to his usual and daily occupation; and that he is and probably will in the future be obliged to expend large sums of money in and about the curing of the aforesaid injuries to his great damage and financial loss. 

8. All and singular the premises are true and within the admiralty and the maritime jurisdiction of the United States and this Honorable Court.

Forms of affidavits and oaths in various proceedings and of various officers, etc., will be found under the appropriate titles. 

An affidavit is an oath or affirmation reduced to writing, sworn or affirmed to before some officer who has authority to administer it. It differs from a deposition in this, that, in the latter, the opposite party has had an opportunity to cross-examine the witness, whereas an affidavit is always taken ex parte. 

An oath is an outward pledge, given by the person taking it, that his attestation or promise is made under an immediate sense of his responsibility to God. Greenleaf on Ev. 328. 

Oaths are taken in various forms: a usual form is upon the 

Gospel, by taking the book in hand; and the words commonly used are, "You do swear that," &c., "so help you God," and then kissing the book. The origin of this oath may be traced to the Roman law; and the kissing the book is said to be in imitation of the priest's kissing the ritual, as a sign of reverence, before he reads it to the people. Rees' Cycl.

In Pennsylvania, by Act of 3d April, 1895, P. L. 32, laying the hand upon an open copy of the Holy Bible is substituted for the old form of kissing the book. 

Another form is by the witness or party promising, holding up his right hand while the officer repeats to him "You do swear by Almighty God, the Searcher of all Hearts, that," &c., "and that as you shall answer to God at the last great day."

In another form of attestation, commonly called an affirmation, the officer repeats, "You do solemnly, sincerely, and truly declare and affirm, that," &c., "And so you affirm," or, "are you content?" The oath may, however, be varied in any other form, in order to conform to the religious opinions of the person who takes it. The Act of 23 April, 1909, P. L. 140, provides that the capacity of any witness to testify in any judicial proceeding shall be in no wise affected by his opinion on matter of religion; that no witness shall be questioned concerning his religious belief nor any evidence be heard on the subject; and that the affirmation may be administered to any witness who so desires, and Ishall have the same effect as the oath. 

Form of Oath by Kissing or Laying the Hand upon the 

Book 

Yo do swear, that

Form of Oath by Lifting up the Right Hand 

You do swear by Almighty God, the Searcher of all 

Harts, that and that as you shall answer to God at the last Great Day. 

So help you God.

Form of Affirmation 

You do slomenly, sincerely, and truly declare and affirm, that - ; and so you affirm. 

In the forms which follow, the first blank space should be filled, according to the mode of administering an oath or affirmation, as follows, viz:

If an oath by kissing or laying the hand upon the Book, fill with "swear."

WITNESSES 

163 

If an oath by uplifted hand, fill with "swear by Almighty 

God, the Searcher of all Hearts."

If an affirmation, fill with "solemnly, sincerely, and truly declare and affirm.' 

And the blank space at the end of said forms should be filled as follows, viz:

If an oath by kissing or laying the hand upon the Book, fill with "So help you God." 

If an oath by uplifted hand, fill with "and that as you shall answer to God at the last Great Day."

If an affirmation, fill with "and so you affirm.” 

Oath of a Witness on a Trial 

You do that the evidence which you shall give to the court and jury, in this issue joined, wherein A. B. is plaintiff and C. D. is defendant, shall be the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. So, &c. 

Oath of Voir Dire 9 You do that you will true answers make to all such questions as shall be asked you by the court, touching the matter now before them. So, &c. 

Where a party prays, upon a trial at law, that a witness may be sworn as to his competency, this is called a voir dire; and if it appears that the witness is competent his testimony is allowed, otherwise not. 3 Blackstone's Com. 332. Oath or Affirmation of Witness, in Oyer and Terminer You do that the evidence you shall give between the Commonwealth and the prisoner at the bar, shall be the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. 

So, &c. 

Oath of a Witness to Grand Jury 

You do that the testimony you shall give to the grand inquest for the body of the county of upon such bills of indictment whereunto you shall be examined, shall be the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

Oath or Affirmation of Interpreter, in Civil Courts 

You do that you will truly interpret between the court, the jury, the counsel, and the witness, in the issue joined, wherein A. B. is plaintiff, and C. D. is defendant. So, &c.

Oath or Affirmation of Interpreter, in Criminal Courts

AFFIDAVIT OF DEFENSE SEE: STATEMENTS OF CLAIM JUDGMENTS-PARTICULAR FORMS OF ACTION 

The Practice Act of 14 May, 1915, P. L. 483, has superseded all acts regulating practice in assumpsit and trespass as defined in the Act of 1887, P. L. 271. Section 12 requires that "the defendant shall file an affidavit of defense to the statement of claim within fifteen days from service thereof." Counties, cities, boroughs, etc., need not do so by virtue of the Act of 1917, P. L. 

150. Affidavits must contain and contain only the material facts relied upon, set forth in a concise and summary form. 

Since the sufficiency of affidavits of defense is nearly always a matter of substantive law, it is obviously impossible to give anything like a complete collection of forms of affidavits. A few typical forms are appended which may be found useful as guides.

(4) certain promissory notes for dollars each which are set forth in plaintiff's statement of claim filed in this cause.

Parol Inducing Agreement 

That before and at the time of the execution of the note, upon which suit was brought, it was agreed by and between the plaintiff and the defendant that deponent was not to be required to pay the said note; but that per centum of the shares of the capital stock of the

Company, the property of the plaintiff, the said Company being a corporation chartered and existing under the laws of the state of should be placed in the possession of the deponent for the purpose of sale, and that as the said shares of stock were sold the proceeds derived from the sale thereof were first to be used to pay the amount of the said note, to wit, dollars, and that so soon as the said note was paid the balance of the proceeds to be derived from the sale of the said stock, so far as was necessary, was to be used in the development and placing upon a paying basis of certain mining claims, situate, etc. (describing them), the property of the plaintiff, it being then and there promised and agreed by the said plaintiff, that the said claims would immediately upon the execution and delivery of the said note be duly transferred and conveyed to the said company, the deed or deeds therefor to be duly recorded in the proper office for the recording of deeds in and for the county of state of

By reason of such refusal by plaintiff to carry out his said promises and agreements, which formed the sole inducement for the execution and delivery of said note, it has been and is impossible for deponent to sell or dispose of any of the shares of stock and deponent is not, under the terms of said promises and agreements, liable upon said note.

Goods Sold and Delivered; Defective Quality; 

Rescission 

The defendants thereupon gave to the plaintiff's said agent, an order for nineteen pieces of gray mixed worsted goods, being the goods mentioned in the plaintiff's statement of claim. The said order for the said goods was given by the defendants in reliance upon the said sample, it being expressly agreed that the said goods were to be like the said sample in every respect and the plaintiff warranted that the said goods would be perfect, fully equal to the said sample and suitable for the purpose for which they were ordered as above mentioned. 9 9 The defendants further allege that in an alleged fulfillment of the said order the plaintiff shipped nineteen (19) pieces of gray mixed worsted goods to the defendant in 19as alleged in the statement of plaintiff's claim, but the defendants deny that the said merchandise was of good merchantable quality, but the defendants allege that the said goods were unmerchantable, were not perfect, were not suited for the purpose of manufacturing ladies' suits, and were not in accordance with the sample, nor up to the sample, but on the contrary, the said goods were unmerchantable, unsuited to the said purpose, imperfect, and that "runners" were found all through the said goods. The defendants further allege that "runners" are heavy threads running through the goods which result from imperfections in weaving and render the goods in question unmerchantable and entirely unsuited for the purpose for which the order was given as aforesaid. The defendants further allege that the said goods were dirty, not in the ordinary sense but in the technical trade sense, that is to say the goods were not of the right color, were not the color of the sample, and were for that reason alone entirely unsuited for use in the manufacture of ladies' suits in filling orders which the defendants had on hand for said suits when the said order was given to the plaintiff.

PARTICULAR MATTERS 

183 The defendants further allege that a few days after receiving the said goods they inspected the same and found thereby that the goods were imperfect and defective as above alleged. Thereupon the defendants returned the said goods to the plaintiff for the season above set forth and made such re-delivery unconditionally and the plaintiff accepted the return of all of the said goods. During the few days in which the goods remained in the possession of the defendants no change was made in them and the defendants exercised no right of ownership in them whatever, and when they were returned as aforesaid to the plaintiff they were in the same condition in which the defendants received them. 

The defendants allege that they are not indebted to the plaintiff for any sum whatever in respect to the said goods or because of any alleged loss by reason of a resale at less than the contract price. The defendants further allege that the said goods had no market value for the defendants' purposes at the time of their delivery to defendants.

(Follow General Form as in Affidavit of Defense.) AGREEMENTS AND CONTRACTS SEE LETTERS OF CREDIT AND GUARANTEES; MARRIAGE, AS TO ARTICLES OF SEPARATION; PARTNERSHIP;  

A CONTRACT is an agreement, upon sufficient consideration, to do or not to do a particular thing. If under seal, it is denominated a specialty, and if not under seal, an agreement by parol; and the latter includes verbal and written contracts not under seal. 

In effect, there is little difference between an agreement in writing without a seal, and one by parol; except that the former can be more easily proved, and is, therefore, to be preferred. 

While not absolutely necessary, it is, in most cases, desirable that written contracts should be under seal. 

Care should be taken to have the agreement or contract clearly expressed. The want of care is a fruitful source of difficulty and lawsuits.

To render an agreement complete, six things must concur; there must be, 1st, a person to contract; 2d, a person able to be contracted with; 3d, a thing to be contracted for; 4th, a lawful consideration; 5th, clear and explicit words to express the agreement; and 6th, the assent of the contracting parties. Consideration is no longer necessary in a written release or promise if there

2. That the First Party shall be permitted, freely and without interference, or hindrance, to enter upon the parcel of land of the Second Party, for the purpose of excavating and constructing the said party wall. 

3. That the said party wall so to be constructed shall not extend nearer the street than the front wall of the building on the easterly side of said parcel of land, from which point it may be extended northerly for a distance not exceeding fifty-five (55) feet; that the party wall so to be constructed shall be laid on good and sufficient bottom stone, which shall be bedded not less than nine (9) feet below the curbstone in front of the dividing line between the said parcels of land; that the foundation of said wall so to be constructed shall be made and constructed of good stone, and shall be not less than twentyfour (24) inches in thickness to the underside of the first tier beams; that, above the underside of the first tier beams, it shall be made and constructed of sound hard brick and shall be not less than sixteen (16) inches in thickness all the way up to the roof of the building of the First Party; and that it shall be extended and constructed to a proper height above the roof of such building, and shall be covered with a proper coping of blue stone. 

4. That, whenever the Second Party shall desire to use said party wall, the Second Party shall pay such proportion of the value of said wall as the portion thereof, which he may use, shall bear to the value of the whole of said wall, and such value shall be ascertained, in the event of a disagreement in respect thereof between the parties, by arbitration; and each party, in the event of

such disagreement, shall choose one disinterested person. 

If those chosen shall be unable to agree, they shall choose a third person to aid in ascertaining and fixing such valuation, and a decision of any two of such persons, shall be binding upon both parties. 

5. That, if either party shall, at any time, desire to raise said wall to a greater height than that to which it may at first be carried, he shall be at liberty to do so, and such additional wall shall be made and constructed by such party wholly at his expense, unless the other party shall desire to use the whole, or any portion, of such additional wall; and, in such a case, such other party shall pay for the same in the manner above provided for the main wall. 

6. That, if it shall be necessary, at any time, to repair, or rebuild, the whole, or any portion, of said wall, the expense of such repairing, or rebuilding, shall be borne equally between the said parties as to such portions of such wall as shall be used in common by them, and the cost of repairing, or rebuilding, the remaining portion thereof shall be borne wholly by the party, who may exclusively use the same. 

7. That, whenever said wall shall be repaired, or rebuilt, it shall occupy the same space and shall be of the same, or similar, materials, and of the same size, as the present wall, unless any law, or laws, hereafter in force and effect, shall require a wall of different dimensions; and in such event, such wall, when so repaired, or rebuilt, shall be of the dimensions required by such law or laws. 

8. That nothing in this agreement contained shall be deemed to vest in either party any part of the fee of the soil upon which the said party wall shall stand. 

9. That this agreement shall be perpetual, and shall bind the parties hereto, and their respective heirs, administrators and assigns.

IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the parties have hereunto set their hands and seals, the day and year first above written.

This agreement, made the day of in the year one thousand nine hundred and by and between A. B. party of the first part (hereinafter designated the contractor), and C. D. party of the second part (hereinafter designated the owner). 

Witnesseth that the contractor, in consideration of the agreements herein made by the owner, agrees with the said owner, as follows:

Article I. The contractor under the direction and to the satisfaction of E. F. & Co., architects, acting for the purposes of this contract as agents of the said owner, shall and will provide all the materials and perform all the work mentioned in the specifications and shown on the drawings prepared by the said architects for the [state the work, and describe the building and its loca-

tion] which drawings and specifications are identified by the signatures of the parties hereto, and become hereby, together with the general conditions annexed hereto, a part of this contract. 

Article II. The architects shall furnish to the con tractor such further drawings or explanations as may be necessary to detail and illustrate the work to be done, and the contractor shall conform to the same as part of this contract so far as they may be consistent with the original drawings and specifications referred to and identified, as provided in Article I. 

It is mutually understood and agreed that all drawings and specifications are and remain the property of the architects, and that all charges for the use thereof and for the services of the architects are to be paid by the owner.

Article III. No alterations shall be made in the work shown or described by the drawings and specifications, except upon a written order of the architects, and when so made, the value of the work added or omitted shall be computed by the architects, and the amount so ascertained shall be added to or deducted from the contract price. In the case of dissent from such award by either party hereto, the valuation of the work added or omitted shall be referred to three (3) disinterested arbitrators, one to be appointed by each of the parties to this contract, and the third by the two thus chosen; the decision of any two of whom shall be final and binding, and each of the parties hereto shall pay one-half of the expenses of such reference.

Article IV. The contractor shall provide sufficient, safe and proper facilities at all times for the inspection of the work by the architects or their authorized representatives. He shall, within twenty-four hours after receiving written notice from the architects to that effect, proceed to remove from the grounds or buildings all materials condemned by them, whether worked or unworked,

217 and to take down all portions of the work which the architects shall by like written notice condemn as unsound or improper, or as, in any way, failing to conform to the drawings and specifications, and to make good all work damaged or destroyed thereby. 

Article V. Should the contractor at any time refuse or neglect to supply sufficient properly skilled workmen, or of materials of the proper quality, or fail in any respect to prosecute the work with promptness and diligence, or fail in the performance of any of the agreements herein contained, such refusal, neglect or failure being certified by the architects, the owner shall be at liberty, after ten days' written notice to the contractor, to provide any such labor or materials, and to deduct the cost thereof from any money then due or thereafter to become due to the contractor under this contract; and if the architects shall certify that such refusal, neglect or failure is sufficient ground for such action, the owner shall also be at liberty to terminate the employment of the contractor for the said work and to enter upon the premises and take possession, for the purpose of completing the work comprehended under this contract, of all materials, tools and appliances thereon, and to employ any other person or persons to finish the work, and to provide the materials therefor; and in case of such discontinuance of the employment of the contractor he shall not be entitled to receive any further payment under this contract until the said work shall be wholly finished, at which time, if the unpaid balance of the amount to be paid under this contract shall exceed the expense incurred by the owner in finishing the work, such excess shall be paid by the owner to the contractor, but if such expenses shall exceed such unpaid balance, the contractor shall pay the difference to the owner. The expense incurred by the owner as herein provided, either for furnishing materials or for finishing the work and any damage incurred through such default, shall be au-

dited and certified by the architects, whose certificate thereof shall be conclusive upon the parties. 

Article VI. The contractor shall complete the several portions, and the whole of the work comprehended in this agreement by and at the time or times hereinafter stated [state the time, and any exceptions, &c.]. 

Article VII. and to render services as understudy for the part of W. J. in the said play, upon the terms herein set forth, and the Actor hereby accepts such engagement on the following terms: 

2.

The date of the first public performance shall be the day of 

19-, or not later than fourteen days thereafter. Employment hereunder shall begin on the date of the beginning of rehearsals and shall continue until terminated by such notice as is herein provided. 

3. The Manager agrees, as compensation for services hereunder, to pay the Actor the sum of $every week from the date of the first public performance of the play. 

4. (a) The Actor, if required, shall give four weeks' rehearsal without pay; if further rehearsals are required, then for each additional week or part thereof, the Manager shall pay the Actor full salary therefor. (b) Rehearsals shall be considered to be continuous from the date of the first rehearsal to the date of the first public performance of the play as provided in paragraph two. (c) If the above play is a musical play, or a spectacular production, then, wherever the word "Four" appears with reference to rehearsals in this contract, the word "Five" shall be substituted. 

5. This contract may before the beginning of rehearsals be terminated as follows:

If this contract be signed and entered into prior to two months of the date mentioned in paragraph two: (a) By either party give the other written notice and making payment of a sum equal to two weeks' salary. 

This contract may, during rehearsals, be terminated as follows and not otherwise: (b) At any time during the first ten days' rehearsals of the Actor by either party giving written notice, if this contract be signed and entered into within two months

EMPLOYMENT 

263 e S b of the date mentioned in paragraph two, except in case the Actor be reëngaged for a part which he has previously played; or (c) At any time after the first ten days' rehearsals of the Actor, by the Manager, by paying the Actor a sum equal to two weeks' salary. (d) The Actor may cancel the contract by giving written notice and paying to the Manager a sum equal to two weeks' salary. (e) If a play be rehearsed less than ten days and abandoned by the Manager, the Manager shall pay the Actor one weeks' salary. 

6. Either party may terminate this contract at any time on or after the date of the first public performance of the play by giving the other party two weeks' written notice. 

7. (a) If the play runs four weeks or less, the Manager may close the play and company without notice, and terminate the right of the Actor to further compensation, except as hereafter provided, provided he has paid the Actor for all services rendered from the date of the first public performance, and in no event less than two weeks' salary. Should the A. E. A. consent, the Manager may reopen the play during the current season, which event he shall offer the Actor a reëngagement under this form of contract upon the same terms and upon acceptance by the Actor enter into with the Actor such contract of reengagement. Should the Manager fail to do this or reopen the play without the consent of the A. E. A., the previous terms of this clause shall not apply to the Actor and Clause 6 shall remain in full force. (b) If the play shall run more than four weeks, the 

Manager shall give one weeks' notice of the closing of the season of the play and company, and thereby terminate the right of the Actor to compensation except for services performed to the date of closing pursuant to such notice.

8. If the Manager is prevented from giving rehearsals because of fire, accident, riot, strikes, illness of star, or prominent member of the cast, Act of God, public enemy or any other cause which could not reasonably be anticipated, or prevented, then the time so lost shall not be counted as part of the four weeks' rehearsal period herein provided. When said time so lost shall exceed two weeks, the Actor shall be free if he so elects. 

9. (a) The Actor shall furnish and pay for such clothes as are customarily worn by civilians of the present day in this country, together with wigs, boots, and shoes necessarily appurtenant thereto. All other clothes, wigs, shoes, costumes and appurtenances and all "properties" of the actress shall be furnished by the Manager. (b) If the Actor be a woman, then the following clause supersedes (a):

In both dramatic and musical companies all gowns, hats and all properties of the actress shall be furnished by the Manager. Footwear and wigs for modern plays to be furnished by the Actress. (c) It is understood that in every case where the Manager furnished costumes and appurtenances under this paragraph of the agreement, if notice of cancellation of this contract be given by such Actor, in that event he or she shall reimburse the Manager for the necessary and reasonable expense to which Manager may be put in altering or rearranging such costumes for his or her successor. 

10. (a) Eight performances shall constitute a week's work. A sum equal to one-eighth of the weekly salary shall be paid for each performance over eight in each week. 

(b) Salaries shall be paid on Saturday night.

If this illness of the Actor should continue for a period of ten days or more, the Manager may terminate the contract. 

15. The Actor agrees to be prompt at rehearsals, to pay strict regard to make-up and dress, to perform his services in a competent and painstaking manner, to abide by all reasonable rules and regulations, and to render services exclusively to the Manager from the date of the

A. is employed and which the Manager individually, or as a co-partner, or through a corporation shall continue throughout the term hereof to be members in good standing of the Actor's Equity Association. In case of a breach hereof the Actor may terminate this agreement forthwith, in which case the Manager agrees to pay the 

Actor all sums due to date of termination, plus his return fare and plus, as liquidated damages (no present basis for calculation existing a sum equal to two weeks' salary. 

18. In event any dispute shall arise between the parties as to any matter or thing covered by this contract, then said dispute or claim shall be arbitrated. The Manager shall choose one arbitrator and the Actor's Equity Association the second. If within three days these arbitrators shall not be able to agree, then, within that time they shall choose a third, who shall not in any way be connected with the theatrical profession. 

If they fail to do so, J. S., or his appointee shall be the third. The arbitrators shall hear the parties and within ten days decide the dispute or claim. 

The decision of a majority of said arbitrators shall be the decision of all, and shall be binding; and said decision shall be final.

The arbitrators shall determine by whom and in what proportion the cost of the arbitration shall be paid. The parties hereby appoint said Board its agents, with full power to finally settle said dispute or claim, and agree

EMPLOYMENT 

267 that its decision shall constitute an agreement between them, having the same binding force as if agreed to by the parties themselves. 

Should suit be brought before the selection of arbitrators, the party sued may (unless he shall have previously refused arbitration at the request of the other party, or neglected to accept same when tendered) at any time after suit and before trial give notice to arbitrate, and then in such case, arbitrators must be chosen as stated hereinabove. 

C. Agreement Hiring Driver and Collector in Laundry Business 

Agreement, made 9 

19—, between City Laundry 

Co., Inc., a corporation, duly organized under the laws of the State of Pennsylvania, and having its principal office at 222 Tree Street, Philadelphia, (herein called the "First Party"), and R. R., residing at

Phila delphia, (herein called the "Second Party"). 

Wherein it is mutually agreed as follows: 

1. The First Party hereby employs the Second Party as a driver, collector, solicitor and canvasser in its laundry business, at a salary of twenty-five ($25) dollars a week, payable at the end of each week, and at a commission of one ($1) dollar for each new customer obtained by the Second Party for the First Party. That, for the purposes of this agreement, a "new customer' shall be one who, at no previous time, shall have been a customer of the First Party 

2. The Second Party hereby accepts the employment aforesaid, and agrees to perform his services to the best of his ability, and to comply with all the rules, orders and regulations, which the First Party may adopt, from time to time; and the Second Party further agrees to devote to such services as much time each and every day as the First Party may require, but not in excess of sixty (60) hours a week.

3. That this agreement may be terminated, at any time, by either party giving two weeks' notice to the other; and the payment, or tender, of two week's wages by the 

First Party to the Second Party shall be equivalent to two weeks' notice. 

4. It is expressly agreed that, for a period of eighteen (18) months after the termination of this employment, for any cause whatsoever, the Second Party will not, directly or indirectly, as employer, employee, or otherwise, engage in the wet wash laundry business, or in any business similar thereto, nor act in aid of the business of any rival, or competing, person, firm or corporation in the same, or a similar, business, in the City of Philadelphia, and that the Second Party will not, at any time, disclose, or furnish, to any person, firm or corporation, other than the officers of the First Party, the names, or addresses, of any of the customers of the First Party, and that the Second Party will not, in any time, solicit, or canvass, the trade, or patronage of the customers of the First Party, or collect, or deliver, laundry to any of them, for any other person, firm or corporation engaged in the wet wash laundry business, or in any similar business.

WHEREAS, the said John Jones is the owner of a farm in the Township aforesaid, and the said Dutton is about to move upon and work the same, Now 

IN RELATION THERETO IT IS HEREBY MUTUALLY AGREED, as follows: 

1. The said Dutton is to live in the house on said farm and is not to take any other family than his own to live with him or in the house; he is to provide his own fuel, and is not to use any from the farm without the consent of said Jones, which, if given, will be in consideration of some return to be rendered therefor. 

He is to cultivate the said farm in a husbandmanlike

EMPLOYMENT 

271 manner; to put in, work, harvest and thresh the crops in good season, and to do all work necessary in marketing the same.

He is to furnish his own horses, wagons, ploughs, and all other tools, implements and machinery for carrying on the farming and work connected therewith, and to pay all bills and expenses for keeping the same in repair; he is to keep the fences generally in repair, and is to make such new fences as may be needed, not exceeding fifty panels, the materials for which are to be furnished by said Jones. 

2. The said Jones is to pay all taxes assessed on the farm, and he is to furnish a sufficient stock of cows, hogs and poultry, which stock is to be kept good, that is, of equal value, from the proceeds of the farm. At the expiration of this agreement, said stock to be valued or sold; and one-half of the excess over cost to be allowed and paid to said Dutton. 

3. Each party to pay for one-half of the seed grain, grass seeds, and also feed if any shall be necessarily bought for the stock. 

4. As many cows to be kept as the farm will profitably bear; in summer not to be overstocked; in winter enough to consume the hay and fodder raised. Dutton's horses as above to be fed from the produce of farm. No hay, straw, corn-fodder, or manure to be sold or removed from the farm. 

5. Each party to have as many potatoes and as much garden produce and fruit (if grown), as he may require for use in his own family. 

6. The produce of the farm, not consumed as aforesaid, to be sold. The property in said produce until sold to be and remain in said Jones. The sales thereof to be by him or subject to his approval and direction. The money therefor to be paid to and received by him; when so received he shall deduct from the same such sums as he may have paid for common expenses under this agreement, and pay over one-half of the remainder to said

Dutton. Settlements of said receipts and expenses to be made monthly. The possession of the farm to be and remain in said Jones, except so far as may be necessary in carrying on the farming operation by Dutton in pursuance of this agreement. 

7. This agreement to continue for one year from the day of next, and thereafter from year to year; but either party may terminate the same at the expiration of the first or any subsequent year, by giving notice to the other party of his intention so to do, months previous to the expiration of the then current year.

WHEREIN IT IS MUTUALLY AGREED, AS FOLLOWS:

2. Such goods shall be delivered into the sole and exclusive possession of the Factor, at premises designated by the Factor, and there shall be placed and maintained in a conspicuous place at the entrance of every building, or place, in, or at, which said goods, or any part thereof, shall be located, kept, or stored, in legible English, a sign which shall bear the following words:

R. R. CO. INC., FACTOR FOR D. CORPORATION 

or such other wording as the Factor may designate. 

3. The Factor shall make advances upon goods delivered to it, to the extent of seventy-five (75%) per cent of the net value of plain goods, and sixty-six and twothirds (66 2/3%) per cent of the net value of fancy goods; and the Factor shall have exclusive possession, supervision, and control of any goods whereon any such advance shall be made. 

4. (a) The Corporation may make sales of the goods so delivered to the Factor, and the Factor shall deliver the goods held by it, upon sales made by the Corporation; but, upon any such sale being made, any and all accounts created by any such sale and delivery of such goods, as and when created, shall belong to, and be the property of, the Factor, to the extent of the lien of such Factor; and, as and when created, such accounts shall be assigned to the Factor, by assignment, in form approved by said Factor, and all invoices to the debtors of the Corporation

EMPLOYMENT 

275 shall contain thereon the words, "Payable only to R. R.

Co., Inc., No.- 

Street, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, to whom this account has been transferred. (b) The Factor shall permit the Corporation to sell said goods, at the Factor's premises, and shall give the Corporation sufficient facilities for transacting its business, and, upon any sale being approved by the Factor, the Factor shall cause the goods to be delivered. (c) The Factor shall furnish fire, sprinkler and burglary insurance for the goods delivered to it, and shall, upon the sale of such goods, furnish the men and facilities necessary for billing, bookkeeping, packing, shipping, and delivering the same. (d) The Factor shall supply, without charge, all local telephone calls, postage, and stationery necessary for the transaction of business, excepting order blanks. (e) All expenses connected with the selling of the goods, except as hereinbefore otherwise stated, shall be borne by the Corporation and the Factor shall not, in any wise, be responsible for any salaries of any employees employed by the said Corporation; but the 

Factor shall, however, advance fortnightly, out of any moneys in its possession, which may then be due to the Corporation, the moneys required for the payment of salaries of employees of the Corporation. 

5. (a) The Factor shall guaranty the payment in full of such accounts for the sale of merchandise as it may approve of and check; provided that all loss under said guaranty of said accounts, to be sustained and assumed by the Factor, shall be limited to one-half of one per cent upon the net amount of sales guaranteed by the Factors, and the Factor shall, at all times, have a general lien upon all goods in its possession, and upon any accounts representing the sale of any such goods, and upon all moneys in its hands, which may be the proceeds of the collection of any accounts, and upon any other property, assets and effects in its possession, for any sums due, to

(b) The guaranty of accounts, which shall be made by the Factor, as aforesaid, shall be a guaranty of the solvency of the customers only, and the Factor shall not be liable upon any such guaranty, in case any account shall not be collected, by reason of the fact that the debtor, or debtors, avoid payment thereof, by reason of any defense to the contract to sell, or contract of sale.

9. In the event of a termination of this contract, either by the lapse of time, or for any other cause, or in the event of the nonpayment of any sum due, or to become due, to the Factor from the Corporation, and if such default in payment shall continue for twenty days thereafter, the Factor shall have the right, in case of such termination and of the nonpayment of any of the liabilities above, or herein, mentioned, to sell and deliver the whole, or any part of the assets, property and effects aforementioned, given to it as security hereunder, at any broker's board, or at public, or private, sale, at the option of the Factor, at any time, or times, thereafter, without advertisement, or notice, and with the right on the part of the Factor to become the purchaser thereof, at such sale, or sales, free and discharged of any equity of redemption; and, after deducting all legal and other costs and expenses of the sale and delivery, the Factor shall apply the residue of the proceeds of such sale, or sales, so made, to pay any, either, or all, of said liabilities, returning the overplus, if any, to the Corporation; but the

7. In the event of the failure or refusal of Grower to deliver said fruit or any part thereof to Company, the exact amount of damages which Company shall have sustained thereby being extremely difficult of ascertainment, Grower shall pay Company on demand, as liquidated damages for services rendered, marketing investigations made, and loss of profits, a sum equal to 85 per cent of the amount receivable by Company on the undelivered portion under Section (a) of article 2, if the delivery and sale had been made in the manner designated herein, and shall also pay all advances and other sums expended or incurred by Company, on behalf of Grower or in connection with said fruit. 8. CLAUSES Clause Permitting Delivery Within Specified Time after Due Date 

Goods shipped within three weeks after specified time of delivery shall constitute good delivery.

CLAUSES 

291 

Clause Governing Extension of Time for Delivery in Absence of Shipping Instructions 

There shall be no extension of time [s] of shipment [s] specified under this contract except as herein provided for, or as hereafter mutually agreed upon in writing; provided that in case of the Buyer's failure to furnish, at least fifteen (15) days before the expiration of contract time of shipment, shipping instructions for shipment within the remaining period of contract time of shipment, and if in such case the seller does not mail or telegraph, at any time on or before the expiration date of the contract time of shipment, notice to the buyer at the buyer's address above given that the seller elects to hold the buyer for breach of contract, then this contract shall be automatically extended as to all the above commodities then unshipped for an additional period of thirty (30) days from the expiration of contract time of shipment.

Clause Permitting Buyer to Fix Place of Delivery 

All merchandise shall be delivered f. o. b., or at warehouse at as may be specified by the buyer. 

Clause Governing Delivery to Consignee Where Freight Is Prepaid by Consignor 

Delivery at place of shipment to carrier, duly consigned, shall constitute delivery to consignee, and prepayment of freight by

Company shall not alter this provision, since prepayment of freight is made solely for the convenience of the consignee. 

Clause Indicating That Time of Delivery Is of the Essence 

Delivery at the time specified in this contract shall be considered as of the essence of the agreement.

Clause Providing for Cancellation upon Failure to 

Deliver Upon failure of the seller to deliver any installment within thirty days from the due date of delivery of such installment, the buyer may, by notifying the seller, in writing within five days after the expiration of such thirty days, cancel all remaining undelivered installments, unless default in delivery is due to conditions beyond the control of the seller as set forth above. 

Clause Providing Optional Remedies for the Buyer upon 

Failure of Seller to Deliver

That if the seller shall fail, for reasons other than fires, strikes, breakdowns, labor difficulties, acts of carriers, or any causes beyond the control of the seller, to make any shipment on or before the expiration of contract time of shipment when shipping instructions are received by the seller at least fifteen (15) days before the expiration date of contract time of shipment, or shall fail, in case of an extension hereof, to make any shipment on or before the extended time of shipment when shipping instructions are received by the seller at least fifteen (15) days before the expiration date of extended time of shipment, then the buyer may, at its option, give written notice to the seller that the buyer elects to treat the seller's failure to make shipment as a breach of this contract, and in case such notice is received by the seller before actual shipment the seller shall be liable to the buyer for breach of contract and shall pay to the buyer on demand any loss to the buyer represented by the difference between the contract price of the commodities to be shipped or delivered and the market price thereof at the time of seller's breach (it being understood that the market price of said commodities at the time of seller's breach is seller's list price in effect at such time

CLAUSES 

293 for said commodities delivered f. o. b., at the same point and with freight charges added at the same rate per cwt. as provided under the paragraph marked "prices" on the front of this contract). In the event the buyer does not elect to treat such failure on the part of the seller as a breach of contract, by written notice received by the seller at any time before shipment, this contract shall be extended so as to include the shipment and delivery when made; provided that the buyer, however, shall be entitled to a credit of ten cents (10c) per barrel on flour and fifty cents (50c) per ton on feed for each thirty-days period of delay or fractional part there until shipment is made.

Cause Requiring Notice of Inability to Deliver 

Whenever the seller is unable to make delivery due to the occurrence of any of the contingencies above mentioned, he shall notify the buyer within ten days after he has knowledge thereof.

Clause Requiring Delivery after Removal of Disability 

If the seller is unable to make delivery at the time specified by reason of fires, strikes, floods, failure of transportation facilities, or for any cause the condition beyond the seller's control, such inability shall not in any wise invalidate this contract, but the seller shall make delivery within thirty days from the termination of the cause or condition responsible for the seller's inability to deliver.

PROVISIONS CONCERNING CLAIMS Clause Limiting Time for Claims 

Any claim for defective material, short weight, or other deficiency in the merchandise shall be made within thirty days after the receipt of the goods.

Another Clause 

The buyer shall examine the merchandise and shall notify the seller, within thirty days after arrival of the goods, of any deficiency which he alleges renders the goods not in accordance with the contract. If such notice is not sent to the seller within the time specified, the said goods shall be deemed to be satisfactory and in accordance with the contract, and the buyer shall be bound to accept the goods and pay for them according to the terms of the contract. 

Clause Requiring Full Payment Without Deduction for Claims 

The Company agrees properly to investigate every claim made as hereinafter provided and will make prompt and fair adjustment thereof if found meritorious. The purchaser, however, shall in every instance pay to the Company the full amount of invoice without any deduction whatever. No allowance for whatever cause made shall have the effect of impairing or affecting any of the provisions hereof nor shall it constitute any precedent for any claim.

Notice of every claim against the Company must be given to its resident manager at the place where the order was given immediately after the arrival at its destination of the car containing the bananas or fruit complained of and a full statement in writing of the basis of every such claim must be filed with such resident manager within 48 hours thereafter. In default of such notice or written statement the company shall have the option of disregarding any such claim. 

All notices of claims filed with such resident managers will be forwarded to the Company in New York for investigation and decision. No representation or agreement made by any resident manager as to the rejection or allowance of any claim will be binding upon the Company.

AMICABLE ACTION SEE JUDGMENTS 

There is, in Pennsylvania, a mode of instituting suits without a service by sheriff, by an amicable agreement, signed by the parties or their attorneys, and filed in the prothonotary's office. 

When entered such action is considered as if it had been adversely commenced, and the defendant had been regularly summoned. It saves the expense of the original writ, and the sheriff's fee for serving it. The writ, however, is supposed in law to be filed. A case may be stated for the opinion of the court in this way, or a judgment entered. When a judgment is entered in this way, the cause of action should always be expressed in the agreement, and it is well that it be attested by two witnesses.

ARBITRATION AND REFERENCE 

An arbitration is the reference and submission of a matter in dispute, concerning property or a personal wrong, to the decision of one or more persons as arbitrators. Their findings are called awards.

Arbitrations are either voluntary or compulsory. The voluntary are those made by mutual consent; and the compulsory are where either party has a right to enter a rule of reference without the consent of the other. Before the revised Act of 1836, a variety of modes of arbitration existed in Pennsylvania. 1st.

Are those made by mutual consent, in which the parties select the arbitrators, and bind themselves by bond to abide their decision; these are made without any rule of court. 3 Bl. Com. 

16. 2d. Those which are made in a cause pending in court by a rule of court, before trial; these are arbitrations at common law, and the award is enforced by attachment. Kyd on Awards

21. 3d. Those which are made by virtue of the statute 9 & 10 

Will. 3, c. 15, by which it is agreed to refer a matter in dispute, not then in court, to arbitrators, and agree that the submission be made a rule of court, which is enforced as if it had been made a rule of court. Kyd on Awards 22. 4th. Those made under the Act of Assembly of 1705. 

The provisions of the Acts of 1705 and 1810, and the English statutes above mentioned, have been incorporated into the revised Act of 1836. The methods of arbitration at this time most usual in Pennsylvania, are those made by mutual consent, in which the parties select the arbitrators, and bind themselves by bond to abide their decision; or those under the Act of Assembly of 16th June, 1836, P. L. 717, which provides for either voluntary or compulsory arbitrations. Either party in a civil suit or action, or his attorney, may enter at the Prothonotary's office, a rule of reference under the said Act of 1836, wherein he shall declare his determination to have arbitrators chosen on a certain day to be mentioned therein, not exceeding thirty days thereafter, for the trial of all matters in variance in the suit between the parties; provided, that the plaintiff shall not enter such rule until he files a declaration or statement of his cause of action. A copy of this rule is to be served on the opposite party, his agent or attorney, at least fifteen days before the day fixed for the appointment of arbitrators. On the day appointed they meet at the Prothonotary's, and endeavor to agree upon arbitrators; if they cannot, the Prothonotary makes out a list on which are inscribed the names of a number of citizens, and the parties, beginning with the plaintiff, alternately strike one of said names at a time from the list, until there are left but the number agreed upon or fixed by the Prothonotary, who are to be the arbitrators. The time of meeting is then agreed upon by the parties, or appointed by the Prothonotary, provided that the time of meeting shall not be less than ten nor more than twenty days after their appointment. The party by whom the rule of reference shall have been entered must procure from the Prothonotary a certified copy of the record, and serve a copy of the same on each of the arbitrators, and also on the opposite party, his agent or attorney, giving ten days' notice previous to the day of meeting. At the time fixed for the meeting, the arbitrators are sworn or affirmed, justly and equitably to try all matters in variance submitted to them, and proceed to hear

VOLUNTARY 

311 and determine the case. Their award is filed in the office of the 

Prothonotary, and has the effect of a judgment, subject, however to an appeal, which may be entered at any time within twenty days after the filing of such award.

There is no compulsory arbitration in the City and County of Philadelphia.

By the Act of May 14th 1874, P. L. 166, all civil suits or cases which the parties may legally by agreement in writing submit to the decision of a Court, the parties may, in like manner, by written agreement, submit the case to the decision of any person learned in the law, who is authorized to act as an attorney in the 

Supreme Court of Pennsylvania. 

The Act of April 25th, 1927, P. L. 381, et seq., provides that a provision in any written contract, except a contract for personal services, to arbitrate any controversy thereafter arising out of the contract or out of the refusal to perform the whole or any part thereof, or a written agreement to submit to arbitration any controversy existing at the time of the agreement to arbitrate, shall be valid, irrevocable and enforceable. The 

Court on application shall stay any proceedings brought in violation of the arbitration agreement. The act provides the procedure in case one party refuses to proceed with the arbitration agreement. If the making of the arbitration agreement or the failure, neglect or refusal to perform the same, is raised as an issue, the Court, if a jury trial is waived, or the jury, shall try the issue, otherwise all other matters in dispute shall be decided in accordance with the arbitration agreement.
