ARREST IN CIVIL CASES CAPIAS AD RESPONDENDUM 

The Capias ad respondendum is an old common law writ used widely by creditors in order to imprison worthless debtors. By the Act of 1842, however, its scope was greatly limited. It can issue only in (1) actions ex delicto, (2) proceedings for contempt, (3) for fines and penalties, (4) for breach of promise to marry, (5) for moneys collected by public officers or for misconduct in office or profession. The writ is original process issued like a summons upon the filing of an affidavit to hold to bail. 

The defendant is taken by the sheriff bodily and may either give bond or move to quash or abate. Married women, ambassadors, etc., witnesses, infants, and freeholders (see 22 C. C. 77) are exempt from capias. 

Special Capias may issue after suit begun (Act of 1836 P. L. 

573).

CAPIAS AD SATISFACIENDUM 

The writ of capias ad satisfaciendum is a final process issued after entry of judgment. Since it involves the incarceration of the defendant, its use has been limited to cases which could have been begun by capias (Act of 1842, P. L. 339). Where the suit was begun by summons, execution will generally issue both in

The Act of Assembly of Pennsylvania, of 12th July, 1842, to abolish imprisonment for debt, and to punish fraudulent debtors, provides that no person shall be arrested or imprisoned on any civil process issuing out of any court of the Commonwealth, in any suit or proceeding instituted for the recovery of any money due upon any judgment or decree, founded upon contract, express or implied, or for the recovery of any damages for the nonperformance of any contract, excepting in proceedings as for contempt, to enforce civil remedies, actions for fines or penalties, or on promises to marry, on moneys collected by any public officer, or for any misconduct or neglect in office, or in any professional employment; in which cases the remedies. remain as they were before the passage of that act. 

The said Act also provides that in all cases where the party to a suit cannot be arrested or imprisoned; that it shall be lawful for the party who shall have commenced a suit, or obtained a judgment in any court of record, to apply to any judge of the court in which the suit shall have been brought for a warrant to arrest the party against whom the suit shall have been commenced, or the judgment shall have been obtained, whereupon the said judge shall require of the said party satisfactory evidence, either by the affidavit of the party making such application or some other person or persons, that there is a debt or demand due to the party making such application from the other party in a suit or judgment, in which affidavit the nature and amount of the indebtedness shall be set forth as near as may be.

If the demand set forth in the affidavit be such that the party could not, according to the provisions of the said act, be arrested, and if the affidavit shall establish to the satisfaction of the judge, one or more of the following particulars, to wit:

That the party is about to remove any of his property out of the jurisdiction of the court on which such suit is brought, with intent to defraud his creditors.

Or, that he has property which he fraudulently conceals: 

Or, that he has rights in action, or some interest in any public or corporate stock, money, or evidence of debt, which he unjustly refuses to apply to the payment of any such judgment or judg-

ments, which shall have been rendered against him, belonging to the complainant:

Or, that he has assigned, removed, or disposed of, or is about to dispose of, any of his property with intent to defraud his creditors: 

Or, that he fraudulently contracted the debt or incurred the obligation respecting which suit is brought. 

It shall be the duty of the said judge to issue a warrant of arrest.

It is required by said act that the above warrant shall be accompanied by a copy of all affidavits presented to the judge, upon which the warrant was issued, which shall be certified by such judge, and shall be delivered to the party at the time of serving the warrant by the officer serving the same. 

The officer to whom such warrant shall be delivered, shall execute the same by arresting the person or persons therein named, and bringing him or them before the judge issuing the warrant, and shall keep him in custody until he shall be duly discharged or committed, as provided in said act. 

On the appearance of the person so arrested before the judge, he may controvert any of the facts and circumstances on which such warrant issued, and may at his option verify his allegations by his affidavit, and in case of his so verifying the same, the complainant may examine him on oath, touching any fact or circumstance material to the inquiry, and the answers on such examination shall be reduced to writing and subscribed by him, and the officer conducting such inquiry shall also receive such other proof as the parties may offer, either at the time of such first appearance or at such other times as such hearing shall be adjourned to, and in case of an adjournment, the judge may take a bond with or without surety for the appearance of the party arrested at the adjourned hearing. 

The judge can discharge or commit to the jail, as the facts in the case may appear; but such commitment shall not be granted if the defendant shall pay the debt or demand claimed with costs of suit, and of the proceedings against him, or give security to the satisfaction of the judge before whom the hearing shall be had, that the debt or demand, with the costs of suit and proceedings against him shall be paid with interest, within sixty days, if the demand be in judgment, and the length of time 12

for stay of execution given by law on debts of like amount has expired, and if the said length of time has not elapsed, then, that the same shall be paid at the expiration of that time, if that shall be sixty days distant from the time of giving said security, and if not, then, that the same shall be paid within sixty days from the time of giving the same. If the demand be not in judgment at the time of giving said security, the day of payment shall be regulated by the same rule, but in no case shall the party be required to give surety for the payment of the debt before the recovering of judgment.

It is further provided that such commitment shall not be granted if the party arrested shall give bond to the complainant in a penalty of not less than twice the amount of the debt or demand claimed, with such sureties as shall be approved by such judge, conditioned that he will not remove any property which he then has, out of the jurisdiction of the court in which suit is brought, with the intent to defraud any of his creditors, and that he will not assign, sell, convey, or dispose of any of his property with such intent, or with a view to give a preference to any credit for any debt, antecedent to such assignment, sale, conveyance, or disposition, until the demand of the complainant, with costs, shall be satisfied, or until thirty days after final judgment shall be rendered in the suit brought for the recovery of such demand; provided, however, that the 10th section of said act shall apply only to cases where the only fraudulent design against the party arrested is, that he is about to remove any of his property out of the jurisdiction of the court in which such suit is brought, with intent to defraud his creditors.

The said act further provides that the commitment shall not be granted if the person arrested shall give bond with securities that he will within thirty days apply by petition to the Court of Common Pleas of the county, or a judge thereof, if not in session, for the benefit of the insolvent laws. For further provisions on this subject, see said Act of 12th July, 1842. P. L. 339.

The following forms are given under this Act of 12th of July, 1842, and may be varied to suit any of the above-mentioned provisions.

DISCHARGE FROM ARREST SEE INSOLVENT; ASSIGNMENT FOR BENEFIT OF CREDITORS 

By provision of the Act of June 1, 1915, P. L. 704, an arrested debtor may petition for discharge from arrest setting forth his inability to pay the debt. Thereupon the court grants a rule to show cause and the defendant enters security to appear. At the hearing all books, etc., are to be produced and all questions put to the defendant are to be answered. The discharge in no way affects the defendant's liability under the judgment.

(Signature of Defendant's Attorney.) (Date.) ASSIGNMENT SEE , ETC.; COLLATERAL SECURITY 

An assignment, in common parlance, signifies the transfer of any kind of property, real, personal, or mixed, and whether the same be in possession or in action.

In a more technical sense, it is usually applied to the transfer of a term of years; but it is more properly used to signify a transfer of some particular estate or interest in lands. The

ASSIGNMENT 

proper technical words of an assignment are assign, transfer, and set over; but the words grant, bargain and sell or any other words which will show the intent of the parties to make a complete transfer, will amount to an assignment. Assignments of interest in real estate, and the like, should be acknowledged and recorded. Notice of an assignment of a chose in action, a legacy, etc., must be given to the debtor or party holding the fund or estate, in order to give priority over a later assignment of which notice is given. Phillips' Estate (No. 3), 205 Pa. 515. The notice should be in writing and give full details of the assignment, or enclose a copy thereof. 

For specific forms of assignment, see appropriate titles, such as GROUND RENTS; JUDGMENTS; LEASES; MORT- GAGES, etc., etc.

ASSIGNMENT FOR BENEFIT OF CREDITORS SEE DEEDS; INSOLVENTS 

Such assignments must be by deed, recorded in the Recorder's office of the county in which the assignor resides, within thirty days after the execution thereof. If not so recorded the assignment is void as against creditors. If the assignment includes land in another county, the deed should also be recorded there, in order to guard against a subsequent conveyance without notice. Where a nonresident of this state is the assignor, the as-

signment may be recorded in any county where the property is situated.

The wages of miners, mechanics, and laborers are preferred, to an amount not exceeding $100 each. Preference is also given, in certain cases, under the Acts of 1872 and 1883, to the wages of miners, mechanics, laborers and clerks, and other employees, not exceeding $200 each. Subject to these exceptions, and to the payment of liens, the proceeds of the property assigned are to be distributed among all the creditors, in proportion to their several demands. 

The assignor usually reserves property exempt from execution, but if such reservation is not inserted in the deed, he may, nevertheless, retain articles of household furniture, and things of domestic use, to the value of $300. 

It is the duty of the assignee to file in the prothonotary's office an inventory of the property assigned, within thirty days after the execution of the assignment, together with his affidavit that the same is a full and complete inventory of all estate and effects, so far as the same have come to his knowledge. The appraisers are to be appointed by the court or by a judge in vacation. When the inventory is filed, the assignee must give bond, with at least two sufficient sureties, to be approved by a judge, in double the amount of the inventory. The Act of 1883 prescribes the condition in the bond. The inventory must include the real estate, as well as personal property assigned. 

Provision is made by the Acts of February 17, 1876, and May 24, 1893, for the sale of encumbered real estate, clear of liens, either at public or private sale. 

See Acts of 1917, P. L. 268; 1921, P. L. 1045.

WITNESSETH: 

WHEREAS, debtor is engaged in the business of selling at retail toys and radio supplies and kindred merchandise at in the City of Philadelphia, State of Pennsylvania, and has become financially embarrassed and is unable to pay his indebtedness in full, and WHEREAS, debtor's assets, if liquidated, without the necessity of Court proceedings, will save his creditors the substantial expenses thereof and the delay usually incident thereto.

Now, THEREFORE, in consideration of the foregoing and of the mutual promises hereinafter contained, the parties hereto do hereby agree, one with the other, as follows: 

1. Debtor hereby bargains, sells, conveys, assigns, transfers, sets over and delivers unto the said trustee, his successors and assigns, all and singular his assets or property of every kind or nature, wheresoever situate and in whosesoever hands the same may be, subject, however,

TO TRUSTEE 

383 to his claim for exemption as provided by law, as is hereinafter more particularly set forth, to have and to hold the same IN TRUST, nevertheless, upon the terms and conditions as hereinafter contained. 

2. Debtor reserves, as his lawful exemption from the sale of his said assets and property to said trustee, his wearing apparel and cash or merchandise to the value of three hundred dollars ($300.00), which said cash or merchandise will be selected by the said debtor and set apart by the said trustee as soon as convenient, but said trustee may, at his option, sell any such merchandise together with the other assets as hereinafter provided and pay to said debtor from the proceeds of said sale the sum of three hundred dollars ($300.00) in lieu thereof. 

3. Said trustee, as soon as convenient, shall sell, dispose of and liquidate all of the assets and property of said debtor either at private or public sale upon such terms and conditions and in such manner as to him may be deemed most advantageous; and he shall collect and recover all outstanding claims and debts due to the debtors. 

4. Said trustee shall forthwith prepare and forward to all creditors of the said debtor notice of the execution of this agreement and the sale and delivery of the assets of said debtor to said trustee in pursuance thereof and shall advise said creditors of the contemplated sale of said assets and the plan of distribution of the proceeds thereof as hereinafter set forth, and shall submit to said creditors a release to be executed by said creditors in consideration of the distribution as herein provided to be executed by said creditors in full settlement and satisfaction of all claims and demands by each of them against the said debtor. 

5. As soon as the aforesaid release has been executed by all creditors, except possibly those creditors whose claims are less than ten dollars ($10.00), said trustee shall forthwith proceed to make distribution of the pro- 13

ceeds of said sale, after the adjustment of all disputes of any kind, as follows: (a) Federal, State and Municipal taxes. (b) The costs, expenses and charges, including reasonable compensation to the trustee and his counsel and to counsel for debtor. (c) Debtor's claim for exemption of three hundred dollars ($300.00) in cash, if the trustee exercises his option to pay the same in cash as hereinbefore set forth. (d) All claims entitled to priority, provided, however, that if there shall be insufficient assets remaining to pay such claims in full pro rata among such claimants. (e) The balance of proceeds remaining to be distributed pro rata among the general unsecured creditors. 

6. The Trustee shall have the right to agree with any creditor upon the amount and/or the order of his priority in payment and when all the said disputes shall be agreed upon the same shall be binding, final and conclusive upon all parties hereto. 

7. Said trustee shall not be chargeable or liable personally for any of his acts or omissions, or the acts or omissions of his attorneys and agents, if in good faith, and shall only be liable for wilful misfeasance or gross negligence in the performance of the duties as herein provided.

ATTACHMENT 

407 

ATTACHMENT 

An ATTACHMENT in criminal-law practice, is a writ requiring the sheriff or other proper officer, to arrest a particular person, who has been guilty of a contempt of court, and to bring the offender before the court.

An attachment in civil-law practice is a writ issued by a court of competent jurisdiction, commanding the sheriff or other proper officer to seize any property, credit, or right belonging to the defendant, in whatever hands the same may be found, to satisfy the demand which the plaintiff has against him. Bouv. 

Law Dic. 

In Pennsylvania there are various forms of the Writ of Attachment in use, the principal of which are-Foreign Attachment, Domestic Attachment, Attachment of Vessels, Execution Attachment under the Act of 16th June, 1836, Attachment against absent and fraudulent debtors, under the Act of 12th July, 1842, and Act of 17th March, 1869, Attachment against 

Witness, &c. 

For the various forms of Writs of Attachment and Docket Entries, before Justices of the Peace and Aldermen, see Binns's 

Justice. 

FOREIGN ATTACHMENT THE FOREIGN ATTACHMENT is a mode of proceeding by a creditor against the property of his debtor. The object of this process is, in the first instance, to compel an appearance by the debtor, although his property may eventually be made liable to the amount of the plaintiff's claim. It is issued solely for the benefit of the plaintiff. 

Under the recent Amendment of 24th April, 1931, P. L. 44, to the original act of 13th June, 1836, P. L. 572, the many prior amendments thereto are codified and the scope of the use of the writ extended. It may now issue in all actions ex contractu and in actions ex delicto for a tort committed in this Commonwealth. 

The persons against whom it may issue are (a) nonresident persons whether in the Commonwealth where the writ issues or not; (b) foreign corporations; and (c) residents removing from the 

Commonwealth after having become liable in an action ex delicto if such removal is to escape service of process. Where there is more than one defendant some of whom are not liable to suit by

ATTACHMENT 

foreign attachment, a clause of summons to such persons may be added to the writ.

The writ is in general terms, not specifying in the body of it the name of the garnishee, or the property to be attached, but commanding the officer to attach the defendant, by all and singular his goods and chattels, in whose hands or possession soever the same may be found, in his bailiwick, so that he be and appear before the court at a certain time to answer, &c. 

If the defendant does not appear the plaintiff files his statement and takes judgment at the third term after issuance of the writ, no service on the defendant of the statement is necessary. 

If the defendant appears or dissolves the attachment judgment for want of an affidavit of defense can be taken 15 days after service of the statement.

The defendant or the garnishee may dissolve the attachment by furnishing bail in double the amount of the claim and the action proceeded in as in assumpsit or trespass. 

If the garnishee appears interrogatories issue to him and judgment accordingly. If the garnishee does not appear a scire facias may issue and if no answer then judgment and execution thereon.

An affidavit of cause of action is required for the issuance of the writ only when it is alleged that a resident defendant has removed from the Commonwealth after becoming liable in an action ex delicto; and when a rule to show cause of action is filed by the defendant or garnishee. It is well however to file such an affidavit in all cases. Particular care should be exercised in drawing it to set forth all jurisdictional facts. The filing of the affidavit, however, does not obviate the filing, within a year of the issuance of the writ, a "statement of cause of action" as required by the Act of 12th May, 1897, P. L. 62, even though the latter be only a verbatum repetition of the affidavit previously filed. Præcipe

DOMESTIC ATTACHMENT 

A DOMESTIC ATTACHMENT is so called because it may issue against persons who are inhabitants, have their domicile, or are domesticated here, in cases where they have been guilty of certain acts of absconding, absenting, or concealment; and is, so far as respects creditors, in the nature of a commission of bankruptcy, because it is for the benefit of all the creditors, and all the property of the debtor is seized and distributed among them pro rata. And the like proceedings may be had if any debtor, not having become an inhabitant of this commonwealth, shall confine or conceal himself within the county, with intent to avoid the service of process and to defraud his creditors. See 

Acts of Assembly, 22d August, 1752, 4th December, 1807, and 

16th June, 1836. 

1. It cannot be issued without oath or affirmation first made. 

2. It is for the benefit of all the defendant's creditors, and not for the benefit of the plaintiff alone.

DOMESTIC ATTACHMENT 

429 3. All the estate of the debtor is vested by the court in three trustees, not being creditors, who must give security for the due execution of the trust, and must make distribution among the creditors. Act of 16th June, 1836, Sects. 13, 15, 19, and 32. 

4. It can only be dissolved by satisfying the court [justice] that the parties were not liable to the attachment. 

5. The law on the subject of domestic attachments is founded altogether upon the Acts of Assembly, which contain comparatively full and precise directions for their regulation. But few decisions are to be found upon their constr ion.

ATTACHMENT AGAINST VESSELS SEE ADMIRALTY 

By the Act of 13 June, 1836, and its supplements, as amended by the Act of 24 June, 1895 (P. L. 251) all vessels built, repaired, fitted, furnished or equipped within this state are subject to a lien for work done or materials furnished and supplies found or provided. This lien is given to all ship-builders, merchants, dealers, tradesmen and mechanics; and it binds the vessel for one year after the work is done or the materials or supplies are furnished. 

There are also acts allowing a lien on vessels navigating the Allegheny, Monongahela, or Ohio rivers, on behalf of employees for their wages, material men, wharfingers, and those claiming damages for breach of certain contracts.

ATTACHMENT 

It must be carefully noted, however, that the jurisdiction conferred upon the state courts by these acts can be exercised by them only in cases which do not fall within strictly admiralty cognizance. Such causes as are within admiralty jurisdiction must be tried in the Admiralty Courts. See The Moses Taylor, 4 Wall. 411; The Lottawana, 21 Wall. 558. 

The practice in this form of proceeding is similar, in many respects, to that pursued, in the Court of Admiralty, for the recovery of seamen's wages, and other debts contracted upon the high seas; and before the abolition of our State Court of 

Admiralty, upon the adoption of the Constitution of the United States, was. precisely similar. 

The whole proceedings are still, however, different from the course of the common law, except that the trial of disputed facts is by jury; these being ascertained, the decree and execution are according to the civil law.

ATTACHMENT AGAINST FRAUDULENT DEBTORS 

Attachment against fraudulent debtors may issue under the Act of March 17, 1869, and its supplements of 1887 for a debt in excess of $100, when the debtor (as verified by affidavit) has or is about to move, conceal, assign or dispose of his assets in fraud of his creditors. Bond must be filed in double the amount involved. Further proceedings are as in foreign attachment except that judgment for want of appearance may be taken against the defendant at or after the second term. *This rule should be allowed by a judge. By it, if the fund is $300, or less, the defendant can obtain it all, without the deduction of a counsel fee for the garnishee.

ATTESTATION is a brief certificate annexed by the witness to an instrument vouching its execution. 

Ordinary Form of Attestation

Where There Are Interlineations in Instruments of 

Signed, sealed, and delivered, in presence of us (the words "and his heirs and assigns" [or whatever they may be] having been previously interlined in the tenth and eighteenth lines from top of second page).

Attestation of an Instrument Executed by a Blind Person The above-written instrument was signed, sealed and delivered by the above-named John Jones, and he being blind, the same was carefully, truly and deliberately read over to him, in presence of us. 

Attestation for a Will

Signed, sealed, published, and declared by the abovenamed John Jones, as and for his last will and testament, in the presence of us, who, at his request, have hereunto subscribed our names at witnesses thereto, in the presence of the said testator, and of each other.

Signed, sealed and delivered by the said A. B., as and for a codicil to be added to and considered as a part of his last will and testament, in the presence of us, who have at his request hereunto subscribed our names in the presence of the said testator and of each other. 

AUDITA QUERELA 

Proceedings by Audita Querela though cumbersome and seldom or never used, can still be utilized. The writ does not issue as a matter of right but solely upon petition to the court.

BAILMENT LEASES 

(See Conditional Sales, Chattel Mortgage, Bills of Sale)

It needs no citation of authority to assure the bar of Pennsylvania of the favored part that the bailment lease has played

BAILMENT LEASES 

in the law. Never having been interfered with by the legislature, there has been thrown around this type of agreement a network of court decisions which have given the lessor rights unheard of in any other system of law. The validity of the bailment lease extends to creditors, heirs, nominees, purchasers and bankrupt estates and by virtue of the Act of 2 June, 1933, P. L. 1417 to landlord's distraints for rent provided written notice of the lease is given within five days after the leased merchandise are placed upon the premises (as to form, see Landlord and Tenant). Even since the Conditional Sales Acts (12 May, 1925, P. L. 603, and 1927, P. L. 979) the bailment lease is still the last word in protection to the lessor or owner (see the recent case of Stern & Co. v. Paul, 96 Super. Ct. 112, 1929.)

82. Motion to Dismiss Specifications of Trustee in Op position to Bankrupt's Application for Discharge 

AND NOW, March 31, 1925, comes Harry Carr by his attorneys, Coke & Littleton, Esqs., and moves the Court to dismiss the specifications of the trustee in the above matter in opposition to the bankrupt's application for discharge, and assigns therefore the following reasons: 

1. The specification alleging the giving of a false financial statement in writing as a ground for refusal of discharge fails to set forth a copy of said alleged financial statement. 

2. The same specification alleges that the financial statement avers the sum of $12,500.00 as cash in bank whereas there was not said sum of cash in bank, but said specification fails to allege what it is claimed was the actual amount of cash in bank. 

3. The same specification alleges that the financial statement avers the sum of $3,400.00 as value of merchandise whereas there was not said merchandise, but said specification fails to allege what it is claimed was the actual value of said merchandise. 

4. The allegation with reference to the alleged concealment of property from the trustee is insufficient in that it fails to set forth any facts which would show a concealment of said property. (Signed) Coke & Littleton, Attorneys for Bankrupt.

(Official character.) BILLS AND NOTES See COLLATERAL SECURITY, for forms of collateral notes. 

The subject of negotiable instruments is now governed by the Act of 16th May, 1901, P. L. 194, 3 Purd. 3252 et seq., which see. 

A BILL OF EXCHANGE is defined to be an open letter of request from, and order by, one person on another, to pay a sum of money therein mentioned to a third person, on demand, or at a future time therein specified. The first party to a bill of exchange is the drawer, or he who makes the order. The drawee is the person to whom it is addressed. The acceptor is he who accepts the bill. The payee is the party to whom, or in whose favor, the bill is made. The endorser is he who writes his name on the back of a bill. The endorsee is one to whom a bill is transferred by endorsement; and the holder is, in general, any one of the parties who is in possession of the bill and entitled to receive the money therein mentioned. 

Bills of exchange are either foreign or inland. All bills which are or purport to be both drawn and payable within the state are inland bills. All other are foreign. Inland bills of exchange are usually denominated drafts, while the term bills of exchange is applied, in commercial parlance, to bills drawn on foreign countries.

Foreign bills of exchange consist, generally, of several parts. 

A party who has engaged to deliver a foreign bill, is bound to deliver as many parts as may be requested. The several parts of a bill of exchange are called a set; each part should contain a condition that it shall be paid, provided the others remain unpaid. The whole set make but one bill. 

There is no precise form of words necessary to a bill of exchange; but to make it negotiable, the power to assign must appear on the face of the instrument; and therefore, a bill drawn payable to A, without the words "or order," "or bearer," is not endorsable over, so as to subject the acceptor to a suit by the endorsee.

The acceptance of a bill of exchange, draft or order must be in writing and signed by the acceptor, or his lawful agent. See 

Act 1901, P. L. 194, Sec. 132.

A PROMISSORY NOTE is defined to be a promise or engagement in writing, to pay a specified sum at a time therein limited, or on demand, or at sight, to a person therein named, or his order, or to the bearer.

The person who makes the note is called the maker, the person to whom it is payable the payee, and the person to whom he transfers the instrument by endorsement the endorsee. 

Promissory notes are negotiable, and when expressed to be "without defalcation," or "without set-off," the endorsee who takes them without notice of defense and before maturity, will not be affected by want of consideration. They may be payable in money, or in a particular kind of current money, or when payable out of the state, with current rate of exchange added: and waiver of exemption law does not destroy negotiability. Nor is negotiability destroyed by provisions authorizing the sale of collateral or confession of judgment. But generally negotiable paper must be simple, certain, unconditional, and not subject to any contingency.

Bills and notes falling due on Sundays, holidays or half holidays, are due on the next secular business day. They are not to be protested on any Saturday, but on the next business day thereafter. Act 1921, P. L. 73, No. 42. 

The following days are holidays, viz: New Year's Day, Lin coln's Birthday (February 12), Washington's Birthday (Feb-

ruary 22), Good Friday, Memorial Day (May 30), the Fourth of July, Labor Day (first Monday in September), Columbus Day (October 12), Election Day, Armistice Day (November 11), Christmas Day, and any day appointed or recommended by the President or the Governor as a day of thanksgiving or fasting. 

All Saturdays are half holidays after 12 o'clock noon. When 

New Year's Day, Lincoln's Birthday, Washington's Birthday, Memorial Day, the Fourth of July, Columbus Day, or Christmas 

Day falls on Sunday, the following Monday is a holiday.

If a seal is added to a promissory note, it is not barred by the Statute of Limitations, which prevents the recovery of a simple contract debt, unless suit be brought, or a fresh promise of payment be made, within six years. A promissory note with a seal attached may now be transferred by a simple endorsement.

ENDORSEMENTS OF PROMISSORY NOTES 

Where the Assignor Is to Be Liable

For value received, I assign the within note to William 

Burns, this day of one thousand nine hundred and 9 and guarantee the collection of the same.

JOHN JONES. 

Where the Assignor Is Not to Be Liable

Without any recourse to me had, I assign, for a valuable consideration, the within note to William Burns, it being the express understanding of the parties, that he takes it at his own risk, and frees me from all responsibilities. 

JOHN JONES. 

The forms given above, for the assignment of a promissory note, are framed to express fully the intent of the assignor; commercial usage, however, has established much shorter forms, which follow, and are equally binding as those above given. 

Short Form, Where the Assignor Is to Be Liable 

Pay to the order of William Burns.

JOHN JONES.

Short Form, Where the Assignor Is Not to Be Liable 

Pay to the order of William Burns, without recourse.

JOHN JONES. 

A JUDGMENT NOTE differs from a common promissory note in having a seal appended with a power of attorney to confess judgment. The maker by the power of attorney, authorizes the payee, or his assigns, to have judgment entered, at any time, against said maker, which is a lien upon his lands, and authorizes the issuing of an execution, whenever said note shall become due and remains unpaid, without resort to a suit to obtain judgment by the ordinary course of law. Judgment notes are now negotiable: Act 1901, § 5, 3 Purd. 3254; but not if they authorize the entry of judgment at any term, whether due or not. 25 Pa. Super. Ct. 494. of

A PRODUCE NOTE is a written engagement to deliver, at a certain place and time, or on demand, specific articles of merchandise, merchandise of a certain general description, at current rates and to a specified value. Such notes, like due bills, are assignable, but not by mere endorsement.

For assignment, with or without liability, the foregoing are suitable; or the following, which is somewhat shorter, will answer: "For value received, I assign the within note, with [or without] recourse, this -day of A. D. 19—.” In an action upon a note for the payment of a certain sum in specific articles, and at a certain place, it is not necessary for the maintenance of plaintiff's action that he should have made a demand of the articles at the time and place; but to defeat the plaintiff's action, the defendant must prove that he was ready at the time and place, and continued ready to deliver said articles. On the failure to make this proof, the plaintiff may recover the amount in money.

PROTEST 1. A PROTEST OF A BILL OF EXCHANGE or PROMISSORY NOTE is a formal declaration made by a Notary Public, at the request of the payee or holder, for the nonpayment of said promissory note, or for the nonacceptance or nonpayment of said bill, protesting that the drawer and all other parties to said promissory note or bill will be held responsible for the exchange, charges, damages, and interest.

As to who may protest for a banking institution, see Acts of 

24 April, 1929, P. L. 651 and 24 March, 1903, P. L. 50.

Notice of protest should be forwarded to the maker or drawer, and to each of the endorsers. 

A party receiving notice of protest is bound to notify those who stand prior to him on the bill, or he loses their security. 

But notice coming from any party to a bill (or his agent, as for instance a notary), will enure to the benefit of every party and operate as a notice from each endorser. 

Protest of a promissory note is not necessary; but notice of nonpayment is necessary to hold the endorsers. 

A foreign bill, appearing to be such on its face, must be protested for nonacceptance and for nonpayment. A bill not appearing to be a foreign bill need not be protested. 

A third person may, after a bill has been protested for nonacceptance, accept it for the honor of the drawer or of any particular endorser. Such acceptance is termed an acceptance supra protest. The acceptor subjects himself to the same obligations as if the bill had been directed to him; but he can recover against the person for whom he accepts and against all who stand prior to him on the bill. 

The following precedents refer to decisions in the courts of Pennsylvania on the more important points of the subject. 

A demand of payment of the drawer, or due diligence in endeavoring to make a demand, is necessary to charge the endorser.

But if the maker has absconded and is not to be found when the note falls due, a demand of payment is not necessary in order to charge the endorser.

Notice of the dishonor of a bill or note must be given in a reasonable time, and by not giving it the holder takes the loss upon himself.

It is settled, that whether or not due diligence was used in making inquiry for the endorser is a mixed question of law and fact. The Court are to give their opinion on the law to the jury according to the circumstances as they appear, but the jury must decide the fact whether there was due diligence or not. 

Putting a letter in the post office will be considered as notice, whether it be received or not, provided it might have reached the person to be affected, in the regular course of mail, but it will be notice only from the time at which it ought to be received.

BILLS OF SALE SEE BAILMENT LEASES, CONDITIONAL SALES. 

A BILL OF SALE is an agreement in writing, under seal, by which a person passes the right or interest he has in goods and chattels. 

As the law imports a consideration when an agreement is made by deed (or seal), a bill of sale, where the property is duly delivered, effects a change of ownership; but a bill of sale is not considered good against creditors where the personal property is retained in the possession of the original owner.

BONDS See ; ATTACHMENT; DECEDENTS' ESTATES; ; FIDUCIARIES; MARRIAGE; 

MORTGAGES; REPLEVIN and see appropriate titles such as 

SHERIFFS, for bonds of various officers.

A bond or obligation is a deed whereby the obligor obliges himself, his heirs, exccutors, and administrators, to pay a certain sum of money to another at a day appointed. If this be all, the bond is called a single bond; but there is generally a condition added, that if the obligor does some particular act, the obligation shall be void, or else shall remain in full force and virtue. 2 Bl. Com. 340. The penal sum in a bond is usually double the amount of the real debt, and is designed to cover the amount of said debt, together with interest and costs. 

A bond, in Pennsylvania, may be transferred under Act of Assembly, by endorsement under hand and seal, in the presence of two witnesses; and in such case the assignee may bring suit in his name.

The assignee of a bond takes it at his own peril. He stands in the same place as the obligee, so as to let in every defalcation which the obligor had against the obligee at the time of the assignment or notice of the assignment, the only intent of the act being to enable the assignee to sue in his own name, and prevent the obligee from releasing after assignment. If the assignee, when he is about to take the assignment, calls upon the obligor to know whether the whole money is due, and the obligor tells him it is a good bond, but is entirely silent as to any claim of his against the bond, he can never after open his mouth against the demand of the assignee. 

Where there is a penal bond with several payments at different times, and the obligor fails to meet any one payment as it becomes due, the obligee can declare on the penalty, and take a

BONDS 

judgment on the whole of the real debt mentioned in the bond, with stay of execution on the several payments, until such payment should become due, as by the conditions of the bond. 

Note should be made of the recent act of 1927, P. L. 985, No. 

475 known as the Uniform Written Obligations Act, providing that: "a written release or promise hereafter made and signed by the person releasing or promising, shall not be invalid or unenforceable for lack of consideration, if the writing also contains an additional express statement, in any form of language, that the signer intends to be legally bound.”

633 Now, THEREFORE, in consideration of the sum of dollars, paid as a premium for the period from to at 12 o'clock noon, and upon the faith of said warranties of said employer as of aforesaid, IT IS HERE- BY AGREED, that, subject to the obligations imposed by this bond on the employer, the performance of which shall be a condition precedent to the right on the part of the employer to recover under this bond, the surety shall, at the expiration of three months next after the surety, shall receive notice of default, reimburse the employer, to the extent of the sum of dollars for such pecuniary loss as the employer shall have sustained of money, securities or other personal property belonging to the employer or in the employer's possession, and for which the employer may be legally liable, caused by any act of larcency or embezzlement upon the part of the employee in the performance of the office or position in the service of the employer hereinbefore referred to, as such duties have been, or may hereafter be stated in writing by the employer to the surety, and occuring during the continuance of this bond, and discovered at any time within six months after the expiration or cancellation of this bond, or in case of the death, resignation or removal of the employee prior to the expiration or cancellation of the bond within six months after such death, resignation or removal. 

The amount of the suretyship hereunder may be increased or decreased, for separate periods, (by rider attached hereto), and this bond may be continued from year to year, at the same or an agreed premium rate so long as the surety shall consent to receive the same, in which event the surety shall remain liable under the terms hereof, between the original date of this bond and the date to which it shall have been continued: PROVIDED, that the aggregate liability of the surety for all defaults of such employee occuring during two or more periods shall not exceed a sum equal to the largest amount of suretyship in force as to such employee during any period within which

BUILDING AND LOAN ASSOCIATIONS See CORPORATIONS; MORTGAGES 

The Building and Loan Code (Act of 5 May, 1933, P. L. 457) provides for the organization and voluntary dissolution of building and loan associations and defines the rights, powers, duties, liabilities and immunities of such associations and of their officers, directors, shareholders, solicitors and other employes. Foreign associations are prohibited from doing business in the Commonwealth.

An association may be formed by fifteen or more incorporators. 

They must all be natural persons of full age and residents of the Commonwealth. At least two-thirds of them must be citizens. The articles of incorporation must be submitted to the 

Department of State and approved by it before a certificate of incorporation may be granted. Appeal lies from the Department's refusal of a certificate to the Governor whose decision is not subject to review.

The shares of the association must have a par value of not less than $100 nor more than $200 but fractional shares may be issued. Shares may be issued in single series, in multiple series or nonserially as provided for in the articles or by-laws. Preferred shares cannot be issued. The association may issue all or any of the following: 1. Installment Shares, to be paid for periodically; 2. Full-paid Shares; 3. Prepaid Shares, on which a part payment is made, the balance to be paid periodically. 

Unpledged shares may be withdrawn at any time by the shareholder. The association at any time may compel the withdrawal of installment or prepaid shares and of full-paid shares of two years standing, provided that there is sufficient cash to pay all

APPLICATION FOR LOAN 

639 such shareholders and provided that all prior shareholders are withdrawn.

Installment or Prepaid shares must be declared matured whenever the payments and earnings thereon properly apportionable thereto equal the par value of the shares. Order of payment and apportionment of funds are treated in section 616 of the code. The powers and limitations of the association are treated in sections 801 to 811; loans to shareholders in sections 901 to 

913; merger and consolidation of associations in sections 1001 to 1010; and voluntary dissolution in sections 1101 to 1113. 

Dissolution and winding-up of associations by the Department of Banking are treated in the Banking Code of 1933.

BULK SALES 

The Act of 23 May, 1919, P. L. 262, known as the "Bulk Sales

Act" deals with the sale in bulk of the whole or a large part of a stock of goods, wares, or merchandise of any kind and/or of fixtures, not in the ordinary course of business. The Act imposes on all purchasers and every auctioneer or agent of the seller, before paying any part of the purchase price or delivering any promissory note or other evidence thereof, the duty to demand of, and receive from the seller or agent a sworn statement of the names and addresses of all the seller's creditors together with the amount due or to become due on account of goods, wares, fixtures or merchandise, or on account of money borrowed to carry on the business of which the goods, wares, merchandise or fixtures being sold are part. The purchaser then must, at least ten days before the completion of the purchase, notify personally or by registered mail each of the creditors. 

Failure to comply with Act makes the sale or transfer fraud-

BULK SALES 

651 ulent and void and the purchaser, auctioneer or agent shall, at the suit of any creditor, be liable to the creditors as a receiver for the fair value of all the property bought or transferred. If the seller and his creditors cannot agree on a schedule of distribution then the purchaser, auctioneer or agent shall pay the money into Court and the Court on motion of any interested party may frame an issue.

No proceeding at law or equity may be brought against the purchaser to invalidate any sale after the expiration of 90 days from the consummation thereof.

The making and/or delivering of a false statement by the seller makes him guilty of a misdemeanor and subject to a fine of $5,000 or 6 months' imprisonment, or both. 

The Act does not apply to (1) sales under order of court, (2) sales by assignees for benefit of creditors, executors, administrators, receivers or any public officer in his official capacity, (3) sales by any officer of a court, (4) sales of furniture, fixtures and equipment of hotels and boarding houses (Act May 10, 1929, P. L. 1710), (5) sales in bulk by a manufacturer of his product (306 Pa. 85) or (6) sales by persons not ordinarily engaged in trade (301 Pa. 31).

The Fiscal Code of 1929 (Act April 9, 1929, P. L. 343), sec tion 1403 provides that every corporation, joint stock association, limited partnership, or company which shall sell in bulk 51% or more of any stock of goods, wares, merchandise, fixtures, machinery, equipment, buildings or real estate, shall give the Department of Revenue 10 days' notice of sale prior to completion of the transfer. It is the duty of the seller to give and the purchaser to require a certificate from the Department of Revenue showing that all State tax reports have been filed and all State taxes paid. The failure of the purchaser to require this certificate renders him liable to the Commonwealth for unpaid taxes owing by the seller or transferer.

CASE STATED

CASE STATED See DECLARATORY JUDGMENTS 

The "CASE STATED" is an agreement in writing between a plaintiff and defendant that the facts in dispute between them are true as therein stated. The facts being thus agreed upon, it is left for the court to decide in favor of which party is the law. 

As no appeal lies on a judgment rendered on a case stated, it is usual in the agreement to insert a clause, that the case stated shall be considered in the nature of a special verdict, or to agree expressly that either party may appeal. 

A case stated must be in a suit actually brought, and it must show a real dispute, not merely a colorable one to obtain an opinion from the court. 

Despite the recent passage of the Declaratory Judgments Act of 1923, P. L. 840 (constitutional, see 284 Pa. 455), the old method of litigation by case stated is still resorted to and found useful. The decided cases should be referred to in such a proceeding (see 86 Super. 256).

A Case Stated 

A. D.

19, it is hereby agreed by and 

And now, between the parties to the above suit that the following case be stated for the opinion of the court in the nature of a special verdict. John Jones, the plaintiff above named, &c., [here state the facts as agreed upon]. 

If the court be of opinion that -, then judgment to be entered for the plaintiff: but if not, then judgment to be entered for the defendant. The costs to follow the judgment, and either party to have the right of appeal to the supreme [or the superior] court.

CERTIFICATES 

A CERTIFICATE is a copy of the record of a Court, duly authenticated; or a writing by which a public officer or other person bears testimony that a certain fact has or has not taken place. 

1 Greenleaf on Ev. 498. 

There are two kinds of Certificates: those required by law, and those which are merely voluntary. Of the certificates required by law, are those given to an insolvent of his discharge, and those given to aliens that they have been naturalized. Voluntary certificates are those which are not required by law, but which are given of the mere motion of the party. The former are evidence of the facts therein mentioned; while the latter,

CERTIFICATES 

which are not unfrequently extorted from weakness or ignorance, are not entitled to any credit, because the facts certified may be proved in the usual way, under the solemnity of an oath or affirmation. 2 Com. Dig. 306; Greenl. Ev. 498.

By the first section of the Act of Congress of the United States, passed March 27, 1804, "All records and exemplifications of office books, which are kept in any public office of any State, not appertaining to a court, shall be proved or admitted in any other court or office in any other state, by the attestation of the keeper of the said records or books, and the seal of his office thereto annexed, if there be a seal, together with a certificate of the Presiding Justice of the court of the county or district, as the case may be, in which such office is or may be kept; or of the 

Governor, the Secretary of State, the Chancellor, or the Keeper of the Great Seal of the State, that the said attestation is given in due form and by the proper officer; and the said certificate, if given by the Presiding Justice of a court, shall be further authenticated by the Clerk or Prothonotary of the said court who shall certify under his hand and the seal of his office that the said Presiding Justice is duly commissioned and qualified; or if the said certificate be given by the Governor, the Secretary of State, the Chancellor, or the Keeper of the Great Seal, it shall be under the great seal of the state in which the said certificate is made. And the said records and exemplifications, authenticated as aforesaid, shall have faith and credit given to them in every court and office within the United States, as they have by law or usage in the courts or offices of the state from whence the same are or shall be taken." 

The second section provides that the first section, above recited, and the Act of 1790, shall apply to books, records, offices, &c., of the territories of the United States, and countries subject to the jurisdiction of the United States. 

By the Act of Congress of 1790, the acts of the legislatures of the several states shall be authenticated by having the seals of their respective states affixed thereto. The records and judicial proceedings of the courts of any state shall be proved by the attestation of the clerk and the seal of the court annexed, if there be a seal, together with the certificate of the Judge, Chief Justice, or Presiding Magistrate, as the case may be, that the said attestation is in due form. Revised Statutes, Sects. 905, 906.

CERTIORARI See , as to certiorari from Supreme or Superior Court. See also WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION. 

A CERTIORARI is a writ issued from a superior court directed to one of inferior jurisdiction, commanding the latter to certify to the former the record in the particular case. 

By the common law, a supreme court has power to review the proceedings of all inferior tribunals, and to pass upon their jurisdiction and decisions on questions of law. But in general the determinations of such inferior courts on questions of fact are conclusive, and cannot be reversed on certiorari, unless some

L 

CERTIORARI 

statute confers the power on such supreme court. 6 Wend. 564; 

10 Pick. 358; 4 Halst. 209. When any error has occurred in the proceedings of the court below, different from the course of the common law, in any stage of the cause, either civil or criminal, the writ of certiorari is the only remedy to correct such error, unless some other statutory remedy has been given. 5 Binn. 

270; 2 Greenl. 165; 8 Ibid. 293. A certiorari, for example, is a correct process to remove the proceedings of a Court of Sessions, or of County Commissioners, in laying out highways. 

Sometimes the Writ of Certiorari is used as an auxiliary process in order to obtain a full return to some other process. 

When, for example, the record of an inferior court is brought before a superior court by appeal, writ of error, or other lawful mode, and there is a manifest defect, or a suggestion of diminution, a certiorari is awarded requiring a perfect transcript and all papers. 

A certiorari cannot be issued from the Supreme Court to a Justice of the Peace in a civil suit. In such case the writ must issue from the Common Pleas (or Municipal Court in Philadelphia County).

A party or his agent or attorney, applying for a certiorari to a justice of the peace, must make affidavit that it is not intended for delay, &c. The writ must issue within twenty days after entry of judgment, unless it be in a case where the justice had no jurisdiction, or where the summons was not served and the defendant did not appear. It must be served within five days, and it is the duty of the party suing it out to serve it and to see that it is duly returned. 

An appeal and a certiorari cannot both be sustained in the same case. A losing party may choose which remedy he will pursue, but he cannot have both.

Answer 

Answer of the defendant county, through its county commissioners.

It is denied that the said plaintiffs have a legal, just and equitable claim for a large sum of money against the county of

It is denied that a strong local prejudice exists against the claim of the plaintiffs, and that the inhabitants of said county, as taxpayers, are prejudiced against the claim of the plaintiffs, and that a fair trial cannot be had in said county.

On the contrary, there is no sentiment whatever among the inhabitants and taxpayers of the said county concerning the claim of the plaintiffs. There has been no public discussion of the claim and no opportunity for prejudice to arise against the claim among the taxpayers of the county. In all the history of litigation against the said county or the municipalities thereof, it has never been the case that local prejudice has existed in favor of the county or the municipality thereof involved and against the claimant bringing suit. On the contrary, it has always been possible to secure a fair and impartial trial in all such cases.

Wherefore affiants pray the Court to dismiss the said petition [or, to discharge the said rule] at the costs of the petitioner.

CHATTEL MORTGAGES SEE BAILMENT LEASES; CONDITIONAL SALES 

CHATTEL MORTGAGES have been given very little countenance in Pennsylvania due particularly to the popularity and extensive use of the Bailment Lease. The legislature has provided however for the use of such defeasible conveyances in certain cases:

LEASEHOLD 

667 (1) by lessee of coal lands or of coal mining rights in Schuylkill County, Act of 1853, P. L. 295; (2) lateral railroads, 1863 P. L. 

532; (3) leaseholds of collieries and manufacturing lands, 1855 

P. L. 368; (4) iron ore, its products and kindred manufactures, 1891 P. L. 102. All such mortgages must be recorded, notice thereof given and under the Act of 1887 shall be valid for only three months unless a statement of the amount due thereon be recorded in that time. 

Any person, association, partnership, or corporation engaged in Pennsylvania in the business of farming or the raising, breeding, fattening or marketing of livestock may borrow funds from any Federal agency now or hereafter authorized to lend money to agricultural producers, or from any bank, trust or savings company, agricultural credit corporation, incorporated livestock loan company, coöperative bank, coöperative crèdit or marketing association entitled to rediscount privileges with the Federal Intermediate Credit Bank under the provision of the U. S. 

Agricultural Credit Act of 1923, and may give as security for such loan a bond containing a confession of judgment secured by a chattel mortgage upon livestock, farm machinery or equipment, or upon any crop planted or to be planted within one year from date of mortgage or any extension thereof. (Seal) COGNOVIT ACTIONEM SEE JUDGMENTS; AMICABLE ACTIONS. 

A COGNOVIT is a written acknowledgment by the defendantsubscribed but not sealed-confessing that the plaintiff's cause of action is just and true; and authorizing the plaintiff to sign judgment and issue execution for a specified sum. Sometimes the defendant confesses a part of the plaintiff's alleged claim, and denies the rest.

COGNOVIT ACTIONEM 

Cognovit in Assumpsit 

(Caption.) 

I confess this action, and that the plaintiff hath [or, 1 confess that I owe to the above-mentioned plaintiff dollars, part of the debt by him in his statement in this action demanded; and that he hath] sustained damages to the amount of dollars, besides his costs and charges, in his behalf, to be taxed by the Prothonotary. 

And in case I shall make default in the payment of the sum of dollars (being the debt in this action), [or if only a part of the claim be admitted, (being so much of said claim as is admitted),] together with the said costs, on the day of next, the plaintiff shall be at liberty to enter up judgment for the said sum of dollars and costs as aforesaid, and sue out execution thereon for the same, together with the amount of official fees, sheriff's poundage, costs of levying, and all other incidental expenses.

And I do hereby agree to withdraw the plea by me pleaded to this action, and undertake not to bring any writ of error in this cause, or do any other matter or thing whereby the plaintiff may be delayed in entering judgment, and suing out execution upon default made as aforesaid.

COMPLAINT COMPLAINT 

Complaint, in criminal law, is the allegation made to a proper officer that some person, whether known or unknown, has been guilty of a designated offense, with an offer to prove the fact, and a request that the offender may be punished.

Although peace-officers are bound, by virtue of their office, to pursue and arrest all persons suspected of crime, with or without a warrant, yet the usual practice is for some one who knows or suspects that another has been guilty of an offense against the common weal, to go to a magistrate, and there lodge his complaint, stating the grounds on which his application is made. 

It should be made on oath or affirmation, and reduced to writing by the magistrate, observing the following directions: It should be correctly dated; contain the name of the place where it is taken, the name and style of the informer, the name of the magistrate and, if possible, of the offender; the time of committing offense, a clear description of it, and the place where it was committed. Upon this the magistrate may issue his warrant or summons, directed to the proper officer, or to any private person by name.

COMPOSITION AND EXTENSION See BANKRUPTCY 

Composition is an agreement, made upon a sufficient consideration, between a debtor and a creditor, by which the creditor accepts a part of the debt due to him, in satisfaction of the whole.

A composition may be made with one member of a firm which has been dissolved, or with one of several joint debtors, and he be released thereby, without thereby releasing the other members of the firm or joint debtors. Act 1862, P. L. 13.

EXTENSION AGREEMENTS 

AN EXTENSION AGREEMENT, also called a "letter of license," is an instrument of writing made by creditors to their debtor, by which they bind themselves to allow him longer time than he had a right to for the payment of his debts; and that they will not arrest, or molest him in his person or property, till after the expiration of such additional time. 

Letter of License from Creditors 

KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS, that we, who have hereunto set our hands and seals, creditors of S. R., has not at present wherewith to pay and satisfy us our several debts, do therefore, upon the request of him, the said S. R., severally and respectively, agree and bind ourselves, our heirs, executors and administrators, to accept and take of him, the said S. R., all such debts and sums of money as he doth owe unto us, and every of us, respectively, by four even and equal payments or portions, that is to say: the first payment to be made in one year next ensuing the date hereof; the second payment in two years next ensuing; the third payment in three years

EXTENSION 

705 next ensuing; and the last payment or residue of such debts to be made in four years next ensuing the date hereof.

And we do further severally and respectively agree not to arrest, sue, implead, attach or prosecute, by any manner of ways or means whatsoever, the said S. R., or his goods or effects, unless default shall happen to be made in payment of the debts aforesaid on the several days and times above limited, under forfeiture and loss of such of our debts and sums of money for which we shall so arrest, sue, implead, attach or prosecute.

(Seal.) CONDITIONAL SALES See BAILMENT LEASES, BILLS OF SALE, CHATTEL MORTGAGE CONDITIONAL SALES have hitherto been an unknown quantity in 

Pennsylvania. The reasons for this condition were (1) the prevalence of the bailment for all purposes which a sale might cover and (2) the fact that the sale invested the vendee with an attachable interest in the property. No protection was afforded the conditional vendor as against either the assignee or the creditor of the vendee. 

On May 12, 1925, however, the legislature passed acts giving conditional sales a legally understandable status. (Act 12 May,

APPLIANCES 

711 

1925, P. L. 603.) (Note: The Act of 1925, P. L. 722, relating to sales of chattels attached or to be attached to realty, was repealed by the Act of 1927, P. L. 979.) It requires the filing in the office of the prothonotary of the contract or a copy thereof in order that it serve as notice to a purchaser or creditor of the vendee. Ten days' grace after the sale is allowed the vendor to file the contract.

Retaking and compulsory resale is allowed by the act after default and 20 to 40 days' notice. If the vendor retakes without notice, he must retain the goods for ten days for redemption by the vendee. Option is also given the vendor to retake subject to no redemption and repay the vendee all payments made. 

The many burdens placed upon the vendor by these acts makes such contracts much less useful than they would ordinarily be expected to be. Full protection can still be had for the vendor by the use of the well established bailment lease (which see). 

The recent case of Stern & Co. v. Paul, 96 Super. Ct. 112, upheld the legality of these instruments despite the acts cited herein. 

By virtue of the Act of 2 June, 1933, P. L. 302, household furniture and goods conditionally sold are exempt from levy and sale by a landlord if notice of the reservation of title is given within 5 days after the goods are placed on the premises (form of notice, see LANDLORD AND TENANT).

CONDITIONS OF SALE 

Conditions of sale are the terms upon which the vendor of property by auction proposes to sell it. 

The conditions for the sale of real estate should be in writing, and the purchaser should sign a written acknowledgment of his purchase. 

A bidder may withdraw his bid at any time before the property is struck off to him.

If a puffer be employed to bid at an auction, it is a fraud on the real bidders and they are not bound. 

An administrator or other trustee, cannot bid or buy at his own sale without leave of the court. If he wishes to buy he should apply to the court for leave to bid. 

Where a buyer at auction fails to complete his purchase, in order to render him liable for loss on resale, the terms of the second sale must not be clogged with terms likely to lower the price.

CONSTABLES 

A CONSTABLE is an executive and ministerial officer of the law within his township, ward, or borough. 

The office is derived from that of the Lord High Constable of England, formerly an officer of great dignity, and vested with high powers to preserve order and enforce the authority of law throughout the kingdom.

CONSTABLES 

The powers and duties of constables relate principally to criminal matters, although, in this country, many duties of a civil nature are by Act of Assembly conferred upon them. Constables are conservators of the peace within their jurisdiction and may apprehend all breakers of the law, and bring them before the proper authorities to answer for their conduct. 

1 Blackstone's Com. 349. It is their duty to keep the public peace in their several districts; and for that purpose they are armed with very large powers of arresting and imprisoning, of breaking open doors, and the like, when such acts are necessary to prevent murder, riots, and violent breaches of the peace. 

1 Penna. Blackstone, 181. 

A constable may, without a warrant, apprehend an offender for treason, felony, breach of the peace, and some misdemeanors less than felony, when committed in his view. 1 Hale, 587; 

1 East, P. C. 303; 8 Ser. & Rawle, 47. But he cannot arrest of his own authority after the affray is over. 2 Camp. 367, 371; 

2 Lord Raym. 1296: 1 Chit. Crim. Law. 20 a 24. 

He may also, upon the information of others, arrest a supposed offender, without any positive charge, on his own knowledge of the circumstances on which the suspicion is founded; but he does so at his peril, unless he can show that a felony has been committed by some person, as well as the reasonableness of the suspicion that the party arrested is guilty. 1 Chit. Cr. 

L. 27; 6 Binn. R. 316; 2 Hale, 91, 92; 1 East, P. C. 301. He has power, also, to call others to his assistance. If a constable have notice that a burglary has been committed, it is his duty to pursue the felon immediately, though in the night. Cro. Eliz. 652. 

At common law, it was the duty of constables to attend the courts of jail delivery and the sessions of the peace for the respective counties, to return warrants and present offenses. 

Cr. Cir. Comp. 34. The duty of attending the county courts is now enforced and regulated, in this country, by statutory provisions.

In Pennsylvania, it was formerly the duty of constables to make returns, on oath or affirmation, to the Court of Quarter Sessions of the proper county, at every term, of all roads in his district which were out of order, index boards to roads not up, bastard children that have been born, and game killed out of

HEAD NOTE 

729 season; of all tippling, disorderly, or gambling houses within said district; of all disturbances of the peace which have occurred at elections; and of all tavern-keepers and retailers of merchandise in said district. The return was presented and sworn to in open court.

The Act of 28 February, 1933, P. L. 5, permits the Court of 

Quarter Sessions in its discretion to regulate or abolish such returns. 

A constable is bound to pursue, search for, and arrest offenders, without other compensation than his legal fees, and cannot recover a reward for arresting a person against whom a warrant has been placed in his hands. 10 Pa. 39.

An action against a constable for an escape is not within the limitation of the Act of 1772. That act protects the officer when acting in obedience to his warrant; not against the consequences of wilful misconduct. 8 Pa. 405.

The refusal, without sufficient excuse, to assist a constable in preventing the escape of a person in his custody, is an indictable offense. 6 Black. 277.

The keeper of a prison is bound to receive a person arrested and brought to him by a constable, and charged with a breach of the peace in his presence. 8 S. & R. 47. 

A constable's return to an execution must be made in writing. 5 W. & S. 457. A constable, neglecting to make return of his execution to the Justice on or before the return day thereof, is absolutely fixed for the debt and costs. 1 Ash. 160. But if the constable does not return it in consequence of the request of the plaintiff, it is "sufficient cause" for not rendering judgment against him. 1 Ash. 160. The mere omission of a constable to return his execution within twenty days, does not fix him for the amount of the debt, if he have sufficient reason for the delay, 6 W. & S. 534. See McClain v. Smith, 4 Clark 452.

If a judgment be rendered against a constable, by a justice of the peace, for neglect of duty, a transcript thereof may be filed in the court of common pleas, and a fieri facias be issued thereon, without an execution having previously issued from the justice. 3 W. 278. 

A constable who levies upon and sells property exempted from execution, is liable to an action, although the time when

CONSTABLES 

the contract (upon which the judgment was founded) was made, was not endorsed upon the execution. 7 Yerg. 88.

A sheriff [or constable] who has legally levied an execution on property bound by a lien, has a right to discharge the lien, in order to get possession; for his writ gives him every implied power which may be necessary to the execution of it. 13 Pa. 

But if he levy on the goods of a stranger, he is not entitled to give in evidence, in mitigation of damages, the payment, out of the proceeds of sale, of a bill for the freight of the goods levied on.

Ibid. 

In an action against the sureties of a constable, upon his official bond, to recover the amount of a judgment for which the constable has become liable, the judgment previously obtained against the constable himself is conclusive evidence of the liability of sureties. 8 W. 398. 

The sureties of a constable are liable for the act of the officer in levying upon the goods of a stranger. 6 W. & S. 513. 

If a warrant appear, on the face of it, to be illegal, the constable is not bound to execute it. 3 Binn. 43.

The same rules of law which govern sheriffs in the execution of process from the higher courts, govern constables in the execution of a justice's process, except where some statute intervenes. 2 Cow. 421. Under the Act 27 April, 1911, a summons may be served by any constable of the county, provided the costs of service shall not exceed what they would have been had the summons been served by "the next constable most convenient.” 

Act of 7 May, 1929, P. L. 1581, gives the Courts of Quarter

Sessions full power, on petition of any citizen of the County verified by affidavit, to inquire into the official conduct of any constable and if the Court is satisfied that such constable is unfit or incompetent to properly discharge his official duties, then said Court may remove the constable and appoint a suitable person to fill the vacancy.

Returns to Executions 

Every execution should, when returned by the constable, be endorsed in such a way that the endorsement may be a proper return to the execution when entered on the docket of the justice. For example, "Money paid into office." "No goods, and defendant not found." "No goods, and defendant by law exempt from arrest." "Levied, and not sold for want of time.' "Levied, and not sold for want of indemnity, the goods levied on being claimed by a third person, D. M." "Levied, sold, and money paid into office." Money paid to plaintiff, whose receipt is on the back of the execution." "Bonded and discharged by the prothonotary." Every return made by the constable should be signed with his name as constable and dated.

CORONER 

The CORONER is an officer of equal antiquity with the sheriff, whose principal duty it is to hold an inquisition, with the assistance of a jury, over the body of any person who may have come to a violent death, or who has died in prison. It is his duty also, in case of the death of the sheriff, or when a vacancy happens in that office, to serve all the writs and processes which the sheriff is usually bound to serve; or when just exception can be taken to the sheriff for suspicion of partiality, as that he is a party to or interested in the event of a suit, &c. 1 Black. 

Com. 349; Bac. Abr. h. t.; 6 Vin. Abr. 242; 3 Com. Dig. 242; 

5 Id. 212. The duties of the coroner are of the greatest consequence to society, both for the purpose of bringing to punishment murderers and other offenders against the lives of the citizens, and of protecting innocent persons from accusations. 

See Bouvier's Law Dict., title "Coroners."

Justices of the peace are also empowered by the Act of 

Assembly of 27th May, 1841, to hold inquests on dead bodies

CORONER 

743 where there is no lawfully appointed coroner, or when he is absent from the county or unable to attend, or where his office is held more than ten miles distant from the place where the death occurred or the body was found. A justice, in such cases, is empowered by said act to select, summon, and compel the attendance of jurors and witnesses, and to receive like fees and tax like costs as a coroner, and the inquest has the same force and effect in law; but said fees or costs are not allowed or paid said justices or inquest until the proceedings are submitted to the court of quarter sessions of the proper county, and the said court has adjudged that there was reasonable cause for holding said inquest, and approved of the same. 

Unless an inquiry shows some reason for supposing a felonious destruction of life, no inquest should be held. Pfout's Case, 7 

Pa. C. C. 265; Bender's Case, 8 Pa. C. C. 664.

A justice's return of inquest must show, on its face, his jurisdiction. In re Cor. Inquest, 2 Del. 446.

Witnesses at an inquest are entitled neither to fees nor mileage. No fees or expenses are allowed the coroner, except as provided by the fee bill, 1 Pa. C. C. 14; 2 Del. Co. 446.

In case of murder or manslaughter, fees, together with mileage from the court-house to the place of viewing the body, are to be paid out of the goods and chattels, lands or tenements of the slayer, if he hath any, otherwise by the county.

In executing processes or writs of any kind, a coroner is allowed the same fees as a sheriff.

CORPORATIONS 

Corporations in Pennsylvania are with very few exceptions formed under the provisions of the Act of 5 May, 1933, P. L. 

364, known as the "Business Corporation Law," and the Act of 5 May, 1933, P. L. 289, known as the "Nonprofit Corporation 

Law." The exceptions are: (1) Coöperative associations, whether for profit or not for profit, (2) any corporation which, by the laws of this Commonwealth, is subject to the supervision of the Department of Banking, the Insurance Department, the Public Service Commission, or the Water and Power Resources Board, and, (3) Beneficial, benevolent, fraternal and fraternal benefit societies, having a lodge system and a representative form of government, or transacting any type of insurance whatsoever. 

A "Business Corporation" is one organized for the direct or indirect pecuniary profit of its shareholders. A "Nonprofit 

Corporation" is one organized for a purpose or purposes not involving pecuniary profit, incidental or otherwise, to its members.

Articles of Incorporation of Business Corporations after ad vertisement are now presented to the Department of State instead of the Governor. The articles, upon being approved and filed by the Department of State, become the charter of the corporation. The Department then issues a "Certificate of Authority" which begins the corporate existence. It is not now necessary to record the articles with the recorder of deeds of the county in which the registered office of the corporation was located. 

A Business Corporation may be formed by 3 or more natural

CORPORATIONS 

persons of full age and either sex, married or single, at least two-thirds of whom are citizens of the United States for any lawful purpose or purposes. Corporations are not now limited to one purpose.

Articles of Incorporation of a Nonprofit Corporation, together with the certificate from the Department of State relating to the registration of the proposed corporate name, are filed with prothonotary of the court of common pleas of the county wherein the registered office of the proposed corporation is to be located. 

The articles and certificate remain there for at least 3 days before an application for a charter is made to the court. The articles are open to public inspection. The incorporators must advertise their intention to apply to the court for a charter. 

On the day specified in the advertisement, or as soon thereafter as the matter may be heard, the incorporators present to the court an application for a charter, the articles of incorporation, proof of the advertisement and the certificate pertaining to the registration of the corporate name. The court may hear evidence or refer the application to a master. If the court finds the articles to be in proper form and within the provisions of the Act, and purposes given in the articles to be lawful and not injurious to the community, the court so certifies on the articles and orders and decrees thereon that the articles be approved. 

Prothonotary transmits the articles to the recorder of deeds for recording. Corporate existence begins upon the recording of the articles. After recording they are returned to the Prothonotary and become part of the records of the court, a certified copy being issued to the incorporators. 

A Nonprofit Corporation may be formed by five or more natural persons of full age and of either sex, married or single, at least 3 of whom are residents of the Commonwealth and citizens of the United States, for any purpose or purposes which are lawful and not injurious to the community. 

Sections 211 to 217 inclusive of the Nonprofit Corporation Law provide for a somewhat different procedure for the incorporation of educational institutions desiring to confer degrees, for certain charitable and eleemosynary institutions, for corporations for the execution of trust instruments, for religious corporations, Young Mens' Christian Associations, cemetery and burial companies, and for incorporation of unincorporated associations.

BUSINESS-NAME
